Poland 
Interior point methods (IPM) were first proposed for linear programming (LP) problems. Since 1984, when Karmarkar published his famous paper (Karmarkar (1984)), IPM were rapidly developed and improved. It is now widely accepted that the primal-dual logarithmic barrier method is the most efficient IPM. The idea of IPM was not restricted to linear programming alone. These methods quickly spread to quadratic, nonlinear and integer programming. The developments in quadratic programming (QP) are closely parallel to those in LP. While theoretical worst-case behaviour for LP and QP are the same, QP problems are harder to solve in practice. The derivation of the higher order primal-dual method for QP is analogous to the derivation for the linear case presented in Mehrotra (1991) and implemented by Altman and Gondzio (1992). 
Let us consider the QP problem 
$$
{ \begin{array} { r } { \operatorname { m i n i m i z e } c ^ { T } x + { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } x ^ { T } Q x , } \\ { { \mathrm { s u b j e c t ~ t o } } ~ A x = b , } \\ { x + s = u , } \\ { x , s \geq 0 , } \end{array} }
$$
where $\mathbf { \Delta } _ { c } , \mathbf { \Delta } _ { x } , s , u \in \mathcal { R } ^ { n }$ , $b \in \mathcal { R } ^ { m }$ and $A \in \mathcal { R } ^ { m \neq n }$ is assumed to have a full row rank. The dual of (1) is given by 
$$
\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { m a x i m i z e } b ^ { T } y - u ^ { T } w - \cfrac { 1 } { 2 } x ^ { T } Q x , } \\ { \mathrm { s u b j e c t ~ t o } ~ A ^ { T } y + z - w - Q x = c , } \\ { x , z , w \geq 0 , } \end{array}
$$
where $\pmb { y } \in \mathcal { R } ^ { m }$ and $\pmb { x } , \pmb { z } , \pmb { w } \in \mathcal { R } ^ { n }$ 
Having incorporated inequality-type constraints in a logarithmic term added to the objective function, we obtain the first order necessary conditions for the optimal solution of (1) and (2): 
$$
\pmb { A x } = \pmb { b } ,
$$
$$
\begin{array} { r } { x + s = u , } \\ { A ^ { T } y + z - w - Q x = c , } \\ { X Z e = \mu e , } \\ { S W e = \mu e , } \\ { x , s , z , w > 0 , } \end{array}
$$
where $x , s , z$ and $W$ are diagonal matrices with the elements $\boldsymbol { x } _ { j } , \boldsymbol { s } _ { j } , \boldsymbol { z } _ { j }$ and ${ \pmb w } _ { j }$ , respectively and $e \in \mathcal { R } ^ { n }$ is a vector of ones. There is only one difference between necessary conditions for LP and QP, namely the term $\boldsymbol { Q x }$ in (5). 
The basic primal-dual algorithm applies one iteration of Newton's method to find an approximate solution to (3-7) for a current (fixed) parameter $\pmb { \mu }$ and terminates when the duality gap is reduced to a predetermined tolerance. It may be viewed as an optimal trajectory from a given starting point to the optimum of (1) and (2). In the Mehrotra method a higher order Taylor approximation of the optimal trajectory is computed. Knowing Taylor terms we can compute the search directions in the primal and dual spaces. 
Undoubtedly, the main computational effort in any IPM implementation is expanded in solving for the direction. To obtain the direction we solve the normal equation with matrix $A ^ { T } \Theta A$ . The difference between linear case and quadratic one is in the matrix $\Theta$ , for the quadratic case 
$$
\Theta = ( Q + X ^ { - 1 } Z + S ^ { - 1 } W ) ^ { - 1 } .
$$
For a linear case $Q = 0$ and other matrices in (8) are diagonal, and computing $\Theta$ is very simple. In many practical problems the matrix $Q$ is either diagonal or we can reformulate the problem (1) to obtain a diagonal quadratic matrix, cf. Vanderbei and Carpenter (1993). Therefore computing $\Theta$ for separable QP is as easy as for a LP. 
The method described above was used for finding cost-effective environmental policy under uncertainty. We considered the problem of reduction of $S O _ { 2 }$ emissions in Europe, cf. Amann et al. (1993). We minimize European-wide emission control costs subject to the condition that grid-specific $s O _ { 2 }$ deposition targets are attained. The costs of emission control are uncertain. There are many possible scenarios of energy production, consumption, fuel characteristics and installed emission control measures. Having scenarios and their probabilities we construct mean-variance model. In such a method we minimize a weighted sum of expected value of total costs and their variance. 
Finally we construct the stochastic optimization problem: 
$$
\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { m i n } E \{ c ( x ) \} + \alpha V \{ c ( x ) \} } \\ { \mathrm { ~ s . ~ t . ~ } T x \leq b , } \\ { l \leq x \leq u , } \end{array}
$$
where $\pmb { c } ( \pmb { x } )$ is a random function and costs are values of this function, $\pmb { x }$ denotes emissions to be reduced, $\pmb { b }$ is a vector of maximal grid depositions, and depositions $\pmb { y }$ are linear function of emissions $\left( { \pmb y } = { \pmb T } { \pmb x } \right)$ . 
The costs for each country are piecewise linear convex functions. Since variance is a quadratic function, the objective function is quadratic too. The problem is reformulated in such a way that the quadratic part of the objective is separable. All constraints are linear. 
To make the model more useful for decision makers we solve the model with different weighting factors for the variance. It enables us to control the value of variance at the solution found; in other words, uncertainty or risk. The method was successfully used at 
IIASA in Transboundary Air Pollution Project. We hope that these ideas can be exploited for a wider class of other stochastic optimization problems.

Preface 
This proceedings volume contains extended abstracts of talks presented at the 18th Symposium on Operations Research held at the University of Cologne, September 1-3, 1993. 
The Symposia on Operations Research are the annual meetings of the Gesellschaft für Mathematik, Ökonometrie und Operations Research (GMÖOR), a scientific society providing a link between research and applications in the areas of applied mathematics, economics and operations research. The broad range of interests and scientific activities covered by GMÖOR and its members was demonstrated by about 250 talks presented at the 18th Symposium. As in recent years, emphasis was placed on optimization and stochastics, this year with a special focus on combinatorial optimization and discrete mathematics. We appreciate that with sections on parallel and distributed computing and on scientific computing also new fields could be integrated into the scope of the GMÖOR. 
This book contains extended abstracts of most of the papers presented at the conference. Long versions and full papers of the talks are expected to appear elsewhere in refereed periodicals. 
The contributions were divided into sixteen sections: (1) Theory of Optimization, (2) Computational Methods of Optimization, (3) Combinatorial Optimization and Discrete Mathematics, (4) Scientific Computing, (5) Decision Theory, (6) Mathematical Economics and Game Theory, (7) Banking, Finance and Insurance, (8) Econometrics, (9) Macroeconomics and Economic Theory, (10) Stochastics, (11) Production and Logistics, (12) System and Control Theory, (13) Routing and Scheduling, (14) Knowledge Based Systems, (15) Information Systems and (16) Parallel and Distributed Computing. 
The conference was opened by the Vice Rector of the University, Professor Speth. Further opening addresses were given by the Vice Mayor of Cologne, Mrs. Canisius, and the chairman of the GMÖOR, Professor Bachem. This year, also the GMÖOR Senior Scientist Prize was awarded during the opening ceremony. The awardee was Professor Krelle, one of the founders of the predecessor organizations of GMÖOR. 
The scientific program consisted of semi-plenary lectures, invited and contributed talks. In the semi-plenary lectures, twelve leading experts gave a one-hour survey on recent developments and most interesting results in their fields. Egon Balas and Joel L. Horowitz started this series with talks on the prize collection TSP and bootstrap methods in applied econometrics. They were followed by Michael Ball who spoke about the design and analysis of reliable networks and by Denis Boyssou with a talk on preference modelling. Rainer Burkard and Bernard Cornet gave talks on the Monge property and exchange economies. Bezalel Gavish surveyed recent results in the area of telecommunication and Jonathan Borwein discussed trends in convex programming. Jan Karel Lenstra spoke about local search methods in job shop scheduling and Robert A. Becker dealt with Ramsey equilibria. The series of semi-plenary talks was closed by David Shmoys and Luk van Wassenhove with talks on the role of linear programming for solving scheduling problems and on recent results in logistics. 
With over 370 participants, about 250 presentations, software demonstrations, press conferences and a lot of other designated actions we were able to show that our field remains active, vital and open for new topics. We would like to thank the authors for presenting their papers and the chairmen of the sections, who helped us in attracting so many distinguished speakers from all over the world. We also thank Dr. Müller of Physica-Verlag for his continuous support and cooperation in publishing this proceedings volume and Mrs. Krupp for her patience and perseverance in preparing its final version. 
The conference was generously sponsored by the Ministerium für Wissenschaft und Forschung des Landes Nordrhein-Westfalen and the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG), which allowed us to support people from abroad and which made it possible that so many authors from Eastern Europe could attend the Symposium. We are deeply indebted to both institutions. 
Finally we would like to thank our university and the members of our organizational staff without whose enthusiastic and unselfish support this symposium would not have been possible.

The Scheduling Problem in High-Level Synthesis: Extended 0/1 LP Model and Solution Methods
Hans Achatz Universität Passau Lehrstuhl Rechnerstrukturen (Prof. W. Grass) D-94030 Passau, Germany 
As demonstrated by the activity in this area high-level synthesis - often referred to as behavioral synthesis - is becoming an increasingly popular research topic. A main part of high-level synthesis is scheduling where each operation from a data flow graph is assigned to a control step besides several constraints. We have formulated the scheduling problem as a 0/1 LP. For the first time we have extended the model to different execution times and multifunctional function units. To decrease the computation time we have developed a method for constructing new lower bounds with the help of LP (!). The results show that computation time is superior to comparable approaches though our model is able to describe a larger set of problems. 
1. INTRODUCTION
High-level synthesis tools transform a behavioral description in terms of algorithm into a RT-level structural description observing several constraints. In order to produce the data path part of a digital processor the following subtasks have to be solved: scheduling, resource allocation and resource binding. This paper is concerned with the scheduling problem as a first step in the sequence of subtasks. Scheduling is the task of assigning operations to control steps optimizing a certain objective function. Several different methods for scheduling have been published. Most of them are heuristics. 
We have extended the $_ { 0 / 1 }$ formulation of Hwang (1991) and Lee (1989) combined with ideas from Gebotys (1991) to enlarge the set of scheduling problems that can be described in our model. These $0 / 1 \ \mathrm { { L P } }$ approaches are very promising with respect to the set of allowable constraints like chaining, multicycle operations, functional pipelining, mutually exclusive operations and loop folding. They also reported very short computing times to get optimal solutions for benchmark examples. However there are at least two drawbacks of these approaches, which are very important for practical applications. They cannot correctly handle multifunctional function units with different operator combinations and they require assigning operation time to operation instances in the behavior description. In practice operation time is a feature of the function unit (FU) or even better of an operation performed by a module. In the second case, different operations of a module for example "add" and "and" may be done in different execution times. The algorithm to be described has been implemented as a part of a high-level synthesis system SUSAN (System for Universal Scheduling and Allocation) (see Achatz (1993b)) transforming VHDL behavioral description into composition of formally verified RT-level modules.

3. GENERATING LOWER BOUNDS VIA LP 
The efficiency of solving the $0 / 1 \bf { L P }$ is extremely dependent on good bounds. In our approach we generate lower bounds via LP. In all applications so far we did not have problems with computing times. For determination of these lower bounds we have to distinguish between time-constrained and resource-constrained scheduling. In the time-constrained model we assume that the number of csteps is given and that we want to minimize the hardware costs. If we know how many units of one type are needed at least the solution space would be reduced. In order to achieve a lower bound for the number of FU-types needed we construct a new objective function 
minimize 
$$
{ \mathfrak { c } } _ { \mathfrak { k } } \cdot \mathbf { M } _ { \mathfrak { k } }
$$
Notice that the objective function only depends on one type of function unit. The problem is solved as LP (!). Therefore computing times are no problem. The solution expresses how many FUs of Type tk are needed at least if all other FU-types do not have any costs. The optimal value of the cost function can be rounded up because the LP solution is always a lower bound for the $0 / 1 \ \mathrm { \bf L P }$ solution. This estimation can be made for every FU-type. So we have generated lower bounds for every FU-type and therefore reduced the solution space drastically. For our experiments most of the lower bounds were also the optimal values. If there are multi-functional FUs with non disjunctive operation type sets the bounds are of course weaker, because one FUtype can replace the other. In a similar way we can compute new bounds for resource-constrained scheduling.

AN APPLICATION OF AN INTERIOR POINT METHOD FOR PROBLEMS WITH UNCERTAINTY 
Anna Altman \*   
Systems Research Institute,

Poland 
Interior point methods (IPM) were first proposed for linear programming (LP) problems. Since 1984, when Karmarkar published his famous paper (Karmarkar (1984)), IPM were rapidly developed and improved. It is now widely accepted that the primal-dual logarithmic barrier method is the most efficient IPM. The idea of IPM was not restricted to linear programming alone. These methods quickly spread to quadratic, nonlinear and integer programming. The developments in quadratic programming (QP) are closely parallel to those in LP. While theoretical worst-case behaviour for LP and QP are the same, QP problems are harder to solve in practice. The derivation of the higher order primal-dual method for QP is analogous to the derivation for the linear case presented in Mehrotra (1991) and implemented by Altman and Gondzio (1992). 
Let us consider the QP problem 
$$
{ \begin{array} { r } { \operatorname { m i n i m i z e } c ^ { T } x + { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } x ^ { T } Q x , } \\ { { \mathrm { s u b j e c t ~ t o } } ~ A x = b , } \\ { x + s = u , } \\ { x , s \geq 0 , } \end{array} }
$$
where $\mathbf { \Delta } _ { c } , \mathbf { \Delta } _ { x } , s , u \in \mathcal { R } ^ { n }$ , $b \in \mathcal { R } ^ { m }$ and $A \in \mathcal { R } ^ { m \neq n }$ is assumed to have a full row rank. The dual of (1) is given by 
$$
\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { m a x i m i z e } b ^ { T } y - u ^ { T } w - \cfrac { 1 } { 2 } x ^ { T } Q x , } \\ { \mathrm { s u b j e c t ~ t o } ~ A ^ { T } y + z - w - Q x = c , } \\ { x , z , w \geq 0 , } \end{array}
$$
where $\pmb { y } \in \mathcal { R } ^ { m }$ and $\pmb { x } , \pmb { z } , \pmb { w } \in \mathcal { R } ^ { n }$ 
Having incorporated inequality-type constraints in a logarithmic term added to the objective function, we obtain the first order necessary conditions for the optimal solution of (1) and (2): 
$$
\pmb { A x } = \pmb { b } ,
$$
$$
\begin{array} { r } { x + s = u , } \\ { A ^ { T } y + z - w - Q x = c , } \\ { X Z e = \mu e , } \\ { S W e = \mu e , } \\ { x , s , z , w > 0 , } \end{array}
$$
where $x , s , z$ and $W$ are diagonal matrices with the elements $\boldsymbol { x } _ { j } , \boldsymbol { s } _ { j } , \boldsymbol { z } _ { j }$ and ${ \pmb w } _ { j }$ , respectively and $e \in \mathcal { R } ^ { n }$ is a vector of ones. There is only one difference between necessary conditions for LP and QP, namely the term $\boldsymbol { Q x }$ in (5). 
The basic primal-dual algorithm applies one iteration of Newton's method to find an approximate solution to (3-7) for a current (fixed) parameter $\pmb { \mu }$ and terminates when the duality gap is reduced to a predetermined tolerance. It may be viewed as an optimal trajectory from a given starting point to the optimum of (1) and (2). In the Mehrotra method a higher order Taylor approximation of the optimal trajectory is computed. Knowing Taylor terms we can compute the search directions in the primal and dual spaces. 
Undoubtedly, the main computational effort in any IPM implementation is expanded in solving for the direction. To obtain the direction we solve the normal equation with matrix $A ^ { T } \Theta A$ . The difference between linear case and quadratic one is in the matrix $\Theta$ , for the quadratic case 
$$
\Theta = ( Q + X ^ { - 1 } Z + S ^ { - 1 } W ) ^ { - 1 } .
$$
For a linear case $Q = 0$ and other matrices in (8) are diagonal, and computing $\Theta$ is very simple. In many practical problems the matrix $Q$ is either diagonal or we can reformulate the problem (1) to obtain a diagonal quadratic matrix, cf. Vanderbei and Carpenter (1993). Therefore computing $\Theta$ for separable QP is as easy as for a LP. 
The method described above was used for finding cost-effective environmental policy under uncertainty. We considered the problem of reduction of $S O _ { 2 }$ emissions in Europe, cf. Amann et al. (1993). We minimize European-wide emission control costs subject to the condition that grid-specific $s O _ { 2 }$ deposition targets are attained. The costs of emission control are uncertain. There are many possible scenarios of energy production, consumption, fuel characteristics and installed emission control measures. Having scenarios and their probabilities we construct mean-variance model. In such a method we minimize a weighted sum of expected value of total costs and their variance. 
Finally we construct the stochastic optimization problem: 
$$
\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { m i n } E \{ c ( x ) \} + \alpha V \{ c ( x ) \} } \\ { \mathrm { ~ s . ~ t . ~ } T x \leq b , } \\ { l \leq x \leq u , } \end{array}
$$
where $\pmb { c } ( \pmb { x } )$ is a random function and costs are values of this function, $\pmb { x }$ denotes emissions to be reduced, $\pmb { b }$ is a vector of maximal grid depositions, and depositions $\pmb { y }$ are linear function of emissions $\left( { \pmb y } = { \pmb T } { \pmb x } \right)$ . 
The costs for each country are piecewise linear convex functions. Since variance is a quadratic function, the objective function is quadratic too. The problem is reformulated in such a way that the quadratic part of the objective is separable. All constraints are linear. 
To make the model more useful for decision makers we solve the model with different weighting factors for the variance. It enables us to control the value of variance at the solution found; in other words, uncertainty or risk. The method was successfully used at 
IIASA in Transboundary Air Pollution Project. We hope that these ideas can be exploited for a wider class of other stochastic optimization problems.

Preface
This proceedings volume contains extended abstracts of talks presented at the 18th Symposium on Operations Research held at the University of Cologne, September 1-3, 1993. 
The Symposia on Operations Research are the annual meetings of the Gesellschaft für Mathematik, Ökonometrie und Operations Research (GMÖOR), a scientific society providing a link between research and applications in the areas of applied mathematics, economics and operations research. The broad range of interests and scientific activities covered by GMÖOR and its members was demonstrated by about 250 talks presented at the 18th Symposium. As in recent years, emphasis was placed on optimization and stochastics, this year with a special focus on combinatorial optimization and discrete mathematics. We appreciate that with sections on parallel and distributed computing and on scientific computing also new fields could be integrated into the scope of the GMÖOR. 
This book contains extended abstracts of most of the papers presented at the conference. Long versions and full papers of the talks are expected to appear elsewhere in refereed periodicals. 
The contributions were divided into sixteen sections: (1) Theory of Optimization, (2) Computational Methods of Optimization, (3) Combinatorial Optimization and Discrete Mathematics, (4) Scientific Computing, (5) Decision Theory, (6) Mathematical Economics and Game Theory, (7) Banking, Finance and Insurance, (8) Econometrics, (9) Macroeconomics and Economic Theory, (10) Stochastics, (11) Production and Logistics, (12) System and Control Theory, (13) Routing and Scheduling, (14) Knowledge Based Systems, (15) Information Systems and (16) Parallel and Distributed Computing. 
The conference was opened by the Vice Rector of the University, Professor Speth. Further opening addresses were given by the Vice Mayor of Cologne, Mrs. Canisius, and the chairman of the GMÖOR, Professor Bachem. This year, also the GMÖOR Senior Scientist Prize was awarded during the opening ceremony. The awardee was Professor Krelle, one of the founders of the predecessor organizations of GMÖOR. 
The scientific program consisted of semi-plenary lectures, invited and contributed talks. In the semi-plenary lectures, twelve leading experts gave a one-hour survey on recent developments and most interesting results in their fields. Egon Balas and Joel L. Horowitz started this series with talks on the prize collection TSP and bootstrap methods in applied econometrics. They were followed by Michael Ball who spoke about the design and analysis of reliable networks and by Denis Boyssou with a talk on preference modelling. Rainer Burkard and Bernard Cornet gave talks on the Monge property and exchange economies. Bezalel Gavish surveyed recent results in the area of telecommunication and Jonathan Borwein discussed trends in convex programming. Jan Karel Lenstra spoke about local search methods in job shop scheduling and Robert A. Becker dealt with Ramsey equilibria. The series of semi-plenary talks was closed by David Shmoys and Luk van Wassenhove with talks on the role of linear programming for solving scheduling problems and on recent results in logistics. 
With over 370 participants, about 250 presentations, software demonstrations, press conferences and a lot of other designated actions we were able to show that our field remains active, vital and open for new topics. We would like to thank the authors for presenting their papers and the chairmen of the sections, who helped us in attracting so many distinguished speakers from all over the world. We also thank Dr. Müller of Physica-Verlag for his continuous support and cooperation in publishing this proceedings volume and Mrs. Krupp for her patience and perseverance in preparing its final version. 
The conference was generously sponsored by the Ministerium für Wissenschaft und Forschung des Landes Nordrhein-Westfalen and the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG), which allowed us to support people from abroad and which made it possible that so many authors from Eastern Europe could attend the Symposium. We are deeply indebted to both institutions. 
Finally we would like to thank our university and the members of our organizational staff without whose enthusiastic and unselfish support this symposium would not have been possible.

The Scheduling Problem in High-Level Synthesis: Extended 0/1 LP Model and Solution Methods
Hans Achatz Universität Passau Lehrstuhl Rechnerstrukturen (Prof. W. Grass) D-94030 Passau, Germany 
As demonstrated by the activity in this area high-level synthesis - often referred to as behavioral synthesis - is becoming an increasingly popular research topic. A main part of high-level synthesis is scheduling where each operation from a data flow graph is assigned to a control step besides several constraints. We have formulated the scheduling problem as a 0/1 LP. For the first time we have extended the model to different execution times and multifunctional function units. To decrease the computation time we have developed a method for constructing new lower bounds with the help of LP (!). The results show that computation time is superior to comparable approaches though our model is able to describe a larger set of problems. 
1. INTRODUCTION
High-level synthesis tools transform a behavioral description in terms of algorithm into a RT-level structural description observing several constraints. In order to produce the data path part of a digital processor the following subtasks have to be solved: scheduling, resource allocation and resource binding. This paper is concerned with the scheduling problem as a first step in the sequence of subtasks. Scheduling is the task of assigning operations to control steps optimizing a certain objective function. Several different methods for scheduling have been published. Most of them are heuristics. 
We have extended the $_ { 0 / 1 }$ formulation of Hwang (1991) and Lee (1989) combined with ideas from Gebotys (1991) to enlarge the set of scheduling problems that can be described in our model. These $0 / 1 \ \mathrm { { L P } }$ approaches are very promising with respect to the set of allowable constraints like chaining, multicycle operations, functional pipelining, mutually exclusive operations and loop folding. They also reported very short computing times to get optimal solutions for benchmark examples. However there are at least two drawbacks of these approaches, which are very important for practical applications. They cannot correctly handle multifunctional function units with different operator combinations and they require assigning operation time to operation instances in the behavior description. In practice operation time is a feature of the function unit (FU) or even better of an operation performed by a module. In the second case, different operations of a module for example "add" and "and" may be done in different execution times. The algorithm to be described has been implemented as a part of a high-level synthesis system SUSAN (System for Universal Scheduling and Allocation) (see Achatz (1993b)) transforming VHDL behavioral description into composition of formally verified RT-level modules.

3. GENERATING LOWER BOUNDS VIA LP 
The efficiency of solving the $0 / 1 \bf { L P }$ is extremely dependent on good bounds. In our approach we generate lower bounds via LP. In all applications so far we did not have problems with computing times. For determination of these lower bounds we have to distinguish between time-constrained and resource-constrained scheduling. In the time-constrained model we assume that the number of csteps is given and that we want to minimize the hardware costs. If we know how many units of one type are needed at least the solution space would be reduced. In order to achieve a lower bound for the number of FU-types needed we construct a new objective function 
minimize 
$$
{ \mathfrak { c } } _ { \mathfrak { k } } \cdot \mathbf { M } _ { \mathfrak { k } }
$$
Notice that the objective function only depends on one type of function unit. The problem is solved as LP (!). Therefore computing times are no problem. The solution expresses how many FUs of Type tk are needed at least if all other FU-types do not have any costs. The optimal value of the cost function can be rounded up because the LP solution is always a lower bound for the $0 / 1 \ \mathrm { \bf L P }$ solution. This estimation can be made for every FU-type. So we have generated lower bounds for every FU-type and therefore reduced the solution space drastically. For our experiments most of the lower bounds were also the optimal values. If there are multi-functional FUs with non disjunctive operation type sets the bounds are of course weaker, because one FUtype can replace the other. In a similar way we can compute new bounds for resource-constrained scheduling.

AN APPLICATION OF AN INTERIOR POINT METHOD FOR PROBLEMS WITH UNCERTAINTY 
Anna Altman \*   
Systems Research Institute,   
Polish Academy of Sciences

Poland 
Interior point methods (IPM) were first proposed for linear programming (LP) problems. Since 1984, when Karmarkar published his famous paper (Karmarkar (1984)), IPM were rapidly developed and improved. It is now widely accepted that the primal-dual logarithmic barrier method is the most efficient IPM. The idea of IPM was not restricted to linear programming alone. These methods quickly spread to quadratic, nonlinear and integer programming. The developments in quadratic programming (QP) are closely parallel to those in LP. While theoretical worst-case behaviour for LP and QP are the same, QP problems are harder to solve in practice. The derivation of the higher order primal-dual method for QP is analogous to the derivation for the linear case presented in Mehrotra (1991) and implemented by Altman and Gondzio (1992). 
Let us consider the QP problem 
$$
{ \begin{array} { r } { \operatorname { m i n i m i z e } c ^ { T } x + { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } x ^ { T } Q x , } \\ { { \mathrm { s u b j e c t ~ t o } } ~ A x = b , } \\ { x + s = u , } \\ { x , s \geq 0 , } \end{array} }
$$
where $\mathbf { \Delta } _ { c } , \mathbf { \Delta } _ { x } , s , u \in \mathcal { R } ^ { n }$ , $b \in \mathcal { R } ^ { m }$ and $A \in \mathcal { R } ^ { m \neq n }$ is assumed to have a full row rank. The dual of (1) is given by 
$$
\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { m a x i m i z e } b ^ { T } y - u ^ { T } w - \cfrac { 1 } { 2 } x ^ { T } Q x , } \\ { \mathrm { s u b j e c t ~ t o } ~ A ^ { T } y + z - w - Q x = c , } \\ { x , z , w \geq 0 , } \end{array}
$$
where $\pmb { y } \in \mathcal { R } ^ { m }$ and $\pmb { x } , \pmb { z } , \pmb { w } \in \mathcal { R } ^ { n }$ 
Having incorporated inequality-type constraints in a logarithmic term added to the objective function, we obtain the first order necessary conditions for the optimal solution of (1) and (2): 
$$
\pmb { A x } = \pmb { b } ,
$$
$$
\begin{array} { r } { x + s = u , } \\ { A ^ { T } y + z - w - Q x = c , } \\ { X Z e = \mu e , } \\ { S W e = \mu e , } \\ { x , s , z , w > 0 , } \end{array}
$$
where $x , s , z$ and $W$ are diagonal matrices with the elements $\boldsymbol { x } _ { j } , \boldsymbol { s } _ { j } , \boldsymbol { z } _ { j }$ and ${ \pmb w } _ { j }$ , respectively and $e \in \mathcal { R } ^ { n }$ is a vector of ones. There is only one difference between necessary conditions for LP and QP, namely the term $\boldsymbol { Q x }$ in (5). 
The basic primal-dual algorithm applies one iteration of Newton's method to find an approximate solution to (3-7) for a current (fixed) parameter $\pmb { \mu }$ and terminates when the duality gap is reduced to a predetermined tolerance. It may be viewed as an optimal trajectory from a given starting point to the optimum of (1) and (2). In the Mehrotra method a higher order Taylor approximation of the optimal trajectory is computed. Knowing Taylor terms we can compute the search directions in the primal and dual spaces. 
Undoubtedly, the main computational effort in any IPM implementation is expanded in solving for the direction. To obtain the direction we solve the normal equation with matrix $A ^ { T } \Theta A$ . The difference between linear case and quadratic one is in the matrix $\Theta$ , for the quadratic case 
$$
\Theta = ( Q + X ^ { - 1 } Z + S ^ { - 1 } W ) ^ { - 1 } .
$$
For a linear case $Q = 0$ and other matrices in (8) are diagonal, and computing $\Theta$ is very simple. In many practical problems the matrix $Q$ is either diagonal or we can reformulate the problem (1) to obtain a diagonal quadratic matrix, cf. Vanderbei and Carpenter (1993). Therefore computing $\Theta$ for separable QP is as easy as for a LP. 
The method described above was used for finding cost-effective environmental policy under uncertainty. We considered the problem of reduction of $S O _ { 2 }$ emissions in Europe, cf. Amann et al. (1993). We minimize European-wide emission control costs subject to the condition that grid-specific $s O _ { 2 }$ deposition targets are attained. The costs of emission control are uncertain. There are many possible scenarios of energy production, consumption, fuel characteristics and installed emission control measures. Having scenarios and their probabilities we construct mean-variance model. In such a method we minimize a weighted sum of expected value of total costs and their variance. 
Finally we construct the stochastic optimization problem: 
$$
\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { m i n } E \{ c ( x ) \} + \alpha V \{ c ( x ) \} } \\ { \mathrm { ~ s . ~ t . ~ } T x \leq b , } \\ { l \leq x \leq u , } \end{array}
$$
where $\pmb { c } ( \pmb { x } )$ is a random function and costs are values of this function, $\pmb { x }$ denotes emissions to be reduced, $\pmb { b }$ is a vector of maximal grid depositions, and depositions $\pmb { y }$ are linear function of emissions $\left( { \pmb y } = { \pmb T } { \pmb x } \right)$ . 
The costs for each country are piecewise linear convex functions. Since variance is a quadratic function, the objective function is quadratic too. The problem is reformulated in such a way that the quadratic part of the objective is separable. All constraints are linear. 
To make the model more useful for decision makers we solve the model with different weighting factors for the variance. It enables us to control the value of variance at the solution found; in other words, uncertainty or risk. The method was successfully used at 
IIASA in Transboundary Air Pollution Project. We hope that these ideas can be exploited for a wider class of other stochastic optimization problems.

Introduction The prevalence of obesity has risen dramatically in the United States and most other economically developed countries in the past several decades (National Center for Health Statistics, 2014; OECD, 2014). Concern about the health risks, medical care costs, and other consequences of obesity has led to a host of policies and programs implemented by companies, school districts, and governments to prevent and reduce obesity. It has also resulted in a large body of economic research on the causes and consequences of obesity and on approaches to prevent and reduce obesity. The purpose of this article is to organize and synthesize what is known from this literature and to identify the most pressing needs and promising opportunities for future research. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the World Health Organization define obesity in adults as a body mass index or BMI (which is calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared) of 30 or higher, and define obesity in youth as a weight-for-height that exceeds the historic 95th percentile (Institute of Medicine, 2012; U.S. DHHS, 2010; WHO, 2000) (see Table 1 for the definitions of each clinical weight classification). BMI does not measure fatness, merely weight for height, so individuals with above-average lean mass (e.g. muscular individuals) may be incorrectly classified as obese (Burkhauser and Cawley, 2008). More accurate measures of obesity are based on fat mass rather than total body mass, and these measures are in some cases more strongly correlated with outcomes than BMI.1 Although a few data sets, such as the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) contain measurements of body composition (such as fat mass and fat free mass), most social science datasets continue to include only weight and height. As a result, most of the research discussed in this review defines obesity using BMI.

Trends in the prevalence of obesity in the U.S. have been tracked for more than 50 years using data on BMI calculated using measured weight and height in the series of NHANES surveys. Americans began gaining weight in the 1920s but this did not result in large increases in obesity until decades later: the 1960s or 1970s if one defines obesity using percent body fat or the 1980s if one defines obesity using BMI (Komlos and Brabec, 2010; Burkhauser et al., 2009). Specifically, the prevalence of obesity (defined using BMI) among U.S. adults rose slowly from $1 3 . 3 \%$ in 1960–1962 to $1 5 . 1 \%$ in 1976–1980. From that point on, it rose dramatically, from $1 5 . 1 \%$ in 1976–1980 to $2 3 . 3 \%$ in 1988–1994 to $3 5 . 3 \%$ in 2007–2010 (National Center for Health Statistics, 2014); see Fig. 1. 2 The prevalence of obesity in youths follows a similar pattern; see Fig. 2. The increase in obesity is particularly striking because it happened at the same time as many healthier trends such as decreased smoking and reduced consumption of alcohol, as well as decreased drug use Source: National Center for Health Statistics (2014), Table 69. among youths (e.g. Stewart and Cutler, 2014; Institute of Medicine, 2012; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2010). Obesity also rose in many other countries of the world during the same period, but the prevalence in the U.S. remains one of the highest. Among the large economically developed countries that are members of The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the U.S. has the highest prevalence of adult obesity $( 3 5 . 3 \% )$ , followed by Mexico $( 3 2 . 4 \% )$ , New Zealand $( 3 1 . 3 \% )$ , Hungary $( 2 8 . 5 \% )$ , Australia $( 2 8 . 3 \% )$ , Canada $( 2 5 . 4 \% )$ , Chile $( 2 5 . 1 \% )$ , the United Kingdom $( 2 4 . 7 \% )$ and Ireland $( 2 3 . 0 \% )$ ; see OECD (2014). 3 East Asian countries such as Japan and Korea have the lowest prevalence $3 . 6 \%$ and $4 . 6 \%$ , respectively); see OECD (2014). The dozen or so countries with higher rates of obesity than the U.S. include small Pacific island nations like Nauru, Tonga, and Samoa, where the prevalence exceeds $5 0 \%$ (World Health Organization, 2011). The Institute of Medicine and the World Health Organization describe current rates of obesity as epidemic (Institute of Medicine, 2012; World Health Organization, 2011). The daily calorie surplus that explains the increase in weights in the U.S. is relatively small: 220 calories per day for adults (Hall et al., 2011) and 41 calories per day for youth (Wang et al., 2012).4 Unfortunately, there are very little direct data on calories consumed and calories burned over time, and what does exist is measured with substantial error. For example, one source of data on calories consumed is from 24-h dietary recall; these were collected as part of the Continuing Survey of Food Intakes by Individuals (CSFII) and continue to be collected as part of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Surveys (NHANES). However, these reports are plagued by significant reporting error. Archer et al. (2013) estimate that food intake in the NHANES is underreported by 281 calories per day for men and 365 calories per day for women (i.e. greater than the calorie surplus that explains the rise in weight over time in the U.S.), and describe the food intake data for a majority of NHANES respondents as “not physiologically plausible” (p. 8), i.e. incompatible with survival. Changes in measurement protocols and potential changes in reporting error over time further complicate efforts to measure trends in energy intake (Archer et al., 2013). Data on calories expended are limited to occasional time use surveys that record only activities, not actual energy expenditure. Data on weight and obesity have their own challenges and limitations. Most datasets used by economists contain only self-reports (not measurements) of weight and height. The NHANES data, which contain both self-reports and measurements of weight and height, indicate that the reporting error in weight is non-classical; specifically, individuals tend to underreport their weight, with heavier individuals underreporting to a greater extent (see, e.g. Cawley et al., 2015).5 Such non-classical reporting error can bias regression coefficients in both models in which weight is the dependent variable and models in which weight is a regressor, and it can be difficult to sign the bias (Bound et al., 2002). One way to address reporting error in weight is to use the NHANES as validation data (Cawley, 2004; Cawley and Burkhauser, 2006; Bound et al., 2002). Specifically, one can regress measured weight on self-reported weight in the NHANES and then “transport” the NHANES coefficients to the dataset of interest and use them to correct self-reported weight for reporting error.6 This assumes “transportability” (that the nature of the reporting error is the same in both datasets) and does not completely eliminate reporting error (O’Neill and Sweetman, 2013; Cawley and Burkhauser, 2006). Estimating models of instrumental variables can also address the Source: National Center for Health Statistics (2014), Table 70. problem of reporting error in weight, but when the error is nonclassical the correction will be incomplete (Bound et al., 2002; O’Neill and Sweetman, 2013). The rise in obesity has serious implications for public health. Excess fat is harmful because fat cells are collectively an endocrine organ, releasing hormones such as resistin, which causes insulin resistance and diabetes, and leptin, which damages the cardiovascular system (Trayhurn and Beattie, 2001; Hu, 2008).7 The pancreas compensates for insulin resistance by releasing even more insulin, which in turn increases the risk of various forms of cancer (Calle and Kaaks, 2004). It is estimated that obesity is responsible for $1 7 . 3 \%$ of coronary heart disease, $6 1 \%$ of Type II diabetes, $2 4 \%$ of osteoarthritis, $2 0 . 8 \substack { - 3 5 . 4 \% }$ of colorectal cancers, $2 6 . 9 \%$ of pancreatic cancer, $3 5 . 5 \%$ of gallbladder cancer, and $4 2 . 5 \%$ of kidney cancer (Eckel, 2003; Calle and Kaaks, 2004). The greatest health impact results from morbid obesity $\left( \mathsf { B M I } \geq 3 5 \right)$ ; those just over the threshold of obesity $3 0 \leq \mathsf { B M I } < 3 5$ , which is called class 1 obesity, do not tend to fare worse than those of healthy weight in terms of medical care costs (Cawley and Meyerhoefer, 2012) or mortality risk (Mehta and Chang, 2009; Flegal et al., 2013). The health impact of morbid obesity is substantial, however, resulting in a roughly onethird higher risk of mortality (Flegal et al., 2013).8 In light of these health consequences, a White House Task Force described obesity as a “national health crisis” for the U.S. (White House Task Force on Childhood Obesity, 2010). Economists took note of the rise in obesity and its implications, and research on the subject increased dramatically. According to the EconLit database of journal articles, dissertations, and working papers, the number of annual economics publications with the keyword “obesity” rose from zero in the year 1995 to four in 2000, 48 in 2005, and 152 in 2010. The economics of obesity, on which there was virtually no research 20 years ago, has become such an active topic that it is challenging to stay abreast of the literature. Given the size of the literature, this review is by necessity selective; for example, it focuses on the studies with the most credible and interesting identification strategies and excludes from consideration unpublished working papers because their results may change. The paper is structured as follows. Section 2 discusses evidence on the economic causes of obesity, such as the money price and time cost of food, food assistance programs, income, education, the macroeconomy, and peer effects. Section 3 discusses the economic consequences of obesity, such as wages, employment, and medical care costs. Section 4 discusses possible mechanisms by which obesity may impose negative externalities and decrease social welfare. Section 5 examines the research on possible mechanisms for internalizing such externalities, and Section 6 discusses the evidence for other economic rationales for government intervention, such as imperfect information and consumers having time inconsistent preferences or behaving irrationally. Section 7 offers an economic research agenda on obesity, noting the greatest needs and most promising opportunities for future research. 2.1. The money price and time cost of food In the past several decades, the real prices of energy-dense foods (i.e. foods with a high number of calories per unit weight) have fallen relative to the prices of less energy-dense, nutritious foods. For example, between 1990 and 2007, the real price of a 2-L bottle of Coca Cola fell $3 4 . 9 \%$ and the real price of a 12-in. pizza at Pizza Hut fell $1 7 . 2 \%$ (Christian and Rashad, 2009) while the prices of fresh fruits and vegetables rose faster than inflation (Wendt and Todd, 2011; Sturm, 2005b). If these types of food are normal goods, then consumers likely responded to these price changes by increasing their consumption of energy-dense foods and decreasing their consumption of fresh fruits and vegetables. A large number of papers have regressed obesity or BMI on local food prices; the limitation of this approach is that variation in local food prices may be due to differences in demand over geography and changes in demand over time and thus the estimates of the impact of local food prices on weight may be biased. A few papers have exploited natural experiments to estimate the effect of food prices on weight. The impact of fast food prices on weight was examined by Cotti and Tefft (2013), which uses the state minimum wage as an instrument for county fast food prices. The logic is that the fast food industry predominantly employs minimum-wage workers, so an increase in minimum wages should to some extent be passed on to consumers in the form of higher food prices. Their IV models (which control for income and employment to address any income effect of minimum wage laws on weight) yield no evidence that fast food prices contribute to obesity; the estimated effects are small, in many cases of the opposite sign than predicted, and statistically insignificant. They also cannot reject the null hypothesis of no effect of their fast food price index on the self-reported consumption of fast food. Others have focused on the price of groceries as opposed to fast food. Courtemanche and Carden (2011) indirectly examine the effect of grocery prices on weight by examining the impact of Wal-Mart Supercenters on the weight of local residents. Wal-Mart has become the largest supermarket chain in the U.S. through aggressive price competition. Generally, the opening of a store would not be useful for identification because it would be a result of demand, but Walmart pursued a strategy of expanding slowly outward in concentric circles from its corporate headquarters in Arkansas. The IV models in Courtemanche and Carden (2011), which use an interaction of distance from corporate headquarters and time as an instrument for the opening of a Wal-Mart store, suggest that an additional Wal-Mart Supercenter per 100,000 residents increases local BMI by 0.24 units, and increases the risk of obesity by $2 . 3 \%$ points, which seems large. These are reduced-form IV models; weight is regressed on the presence of a Wal-Mart Superstore without observing the intermediate steps of grocery purchases or food consumption. Others have studied the influence of the time cost of acquiring fast food, measured by proximity to fast food outlets. Two studies use features of the interstate highway system as instruments for fast food density or distance in order to estimate the causal effects of fast food availability on weight. Dunn (2010) uses the number of interstate highway exits as an instrument for number of fast food restaurants in a county, with the rationale that nearby highway exit ramps imply more visitor traffic that supports additional fast food outlets for reasons that have nothing to do with the demand of residents. Dunn (2010) cannot reject the null hypothesis of no impact of availability or density of fast food outlets on the BMI of white residents in low-density or high-density counties, but finds some evidence that the number of outlets increases BMI among women and non-whites in medium-density counties. Anderson and Matsa (2011) use a somewhat similar approach, using distance to an interstate highway as an instrument for the distance to fast food restaurants, at a fine level of geographic detail (area code and exchange, and zip code) in rural counties of 11 states. The twosample IV models yield no evidence that restaurant access affects BMI, obesity, or overweight; the authors examine food diary data and conclude that the increased calorie consumption from restaurant meals is offset with lower calorie consumption over the rest of the day. Currie et al. (2010) examine the association of schoolchild obesity and the school’s proximity to fast food restaurants. Two strengths of the study are the large sample size (over 3 million ninth-graders in California) and data on measured body fat. The authors compare students whose schools are within 0.1 mile, to those whose schools are within 0.25 mile, of a fast food restaurant and find that students whose school is closer to a fast food restaurant have a prevalence of obesity (defined using body fat) that is $1 . 7 \%$ points $( 5 . 2 \% )$ higher. They estimate that this is consistent with an additional 30–100 calories consumed per school day, which seems large as an intention to treat estimate – the number of additional calories consumed by the children who actually eat at the fast food restaurant that day must be much larger, especially when one allows for some degree of offsetting behavior (eating less at other times of day as a result). There is no difference in the prevalence of obesity between students who attend schools that are 0.25 miles compared to 0.5 miles from a fast food restaurant; it is unclear whether this should be reason for skepticism about the earlier result, or should be interpreted as an indication of the degree of proximity that matters. The authors acknowledge that they have no exogenous variation in distance to fast food restaurants, and thus the estimates could be biased by unmeasured differences in the demand for fast food. They argue that this bias is relatively small for several reasons: they are comparing small distances, a falsification test indicates that proximity to new future fast food restaurants is not associated with obesity, and proximity to nonfast-food restaurants is uncorrelated with weight. The results of these studies are inconsistent; overall, there is weak evidence that cheaper food (in terms of money price or time cost) contributes to obesity. However, this literature is limited by a scarcity of powerful and valid instruments for prices and time costs and generally missing data on the intermediate step of food consumption. 2.2. Food assistance programs The U.S. has many government programs that subsidize food, such as the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), the National School Lunch Program (NSLP), and the School Breakfast Program (SBP). Although they were originally designed to reduce hunger and under-nutrition, they may have the unintended consequence of increasing obesity for certain individuals. For example, benefits in the SNAP program can be spent on the full range of groceries; only prepared food (such as hot rotisserie chicken or sandwiches) and alcohol are excluded, which means that the program subsidizes energy-dense (as well as other) groceries. For example, grocery store scanner data suggest that SNAP pays for roughly $\$ 2$ billion worth of sugar-sweetened beverages annually (Andreyeva et al., 2012). The National School Lunch Program (NSLP) may also have unintended consequences. Part of the motivation for the NSLP was that many U.S. draftees during World War II were rejected for being stunted or malnourished; subsidized school lunches were seen as a way to increase the weight and height of American youth and thereby increase national security by ensuring a larger supply of healthy potential soldiers during the Cold War. Ironically, the NSLP has recently been criticized by the military for increasing youth obesity and thereby decreasing military readiness (Mission: Readiness, 2010). A large number of studies have examined the association of participation in these programs with obesity. However, it has proven challenging to identify the causal effect of the NSLP and SNAP on obesity because there has not been random assignment to the programs and it is difficult to observe a valid control group (Meyerhoefer and Yang, 2011). Studies employing creative identification strategies provide important information on the effects of these programs. For example, Schanzenbach (2009) estimates a regression discontinuity model that compares children whose family income is just below $1 8 5 \%$ of the Federal Poverty Line (and who thus are eligible for subsidized school lunches) to those whose family income is just above that threshold (who must pay full price for a school lunch). Clearly, the running variable (income) may directly affect weight but income is assumed to affect weight in a smooth manner, and not discontinuously at the eligibility cutoff for school lunch. Dividing the estimated impact of eligibility on weight outcomes by the estimated increase in school lunch take-up around the threshold, Schanzenbach estimates that school lunch increases the likelihood of obesity by $4 3 \%$ by the end of first grade. (A Wald estimator calculated using the mean difference in lunch eating rates on either side of the subsidy cutoff implies that school lunch increases the risk of obesity by less – $2 0 \%$ .) These large estimates may be due to the youths’ families becoming eligible for other programs (such as school breakfast) at the same income cutoff. In contrast to these results for first grade, there is no significant impact of the NSLP on obesity at the end of fifth grade. Bhattacharya et al. (2006) estimate the impact of the School Breakfast Program (SBP) using a difference-in-differences model that compares the difference in nutritional outcomes between the school year and summer for students at schools that do and do not offer the SBP. The estimates suggest that the SBP does not increase total calories (it actually decreases calories from fat) but does improve the nutritional quality of children’s diets. Given that their identification strategy relies on relatively short-term seasonal variation, they do not expect to detect an impact on BMI and in fact do not. Millimet et al. (2010) examine the relationship between participation in both the NSLP and the SBP during the spring of 1st grade on weight in the spring of 3rd grade using data from the Early Childhood Longitudinal Study – Kindergarten Class of 1998–1999. Estimates from bivariate probit models with different assumptions about selection into the program suggest that even a modest amount of selection implies that the SBP lowers weight and the NSLP raises child weight, which is generally consistent with both Schanzenbach (2009) and Bhattacharya et al. (2006). Meyerhoefer and Pylypchuk (2008) investigate the relationship between SNAP receipt and obesity using the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey. In order to account for non-random selection into SNAP they incorporate instruments that measure state-level outreach program expenditures for SNAP into a discrete factor model that controls for unobserved heterogeneity. They find no relationship between SNAP receipt and obesity among men, but their estimates suggest that SNAP participation raises the probability of overweight and obesity by $5 . 9 \%$ among women. Kaushal (2007) estimates the impact of SNAP receipt on one specific population – immigrants – by exploiting the fact that after the 1996 Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act (PRWORA), foreign born unmarried mothers’ eligibility for food stamps varied across states and over time. Kaushal estimates a two-sample model of instrumental variables that exploits this policy variation; the estimates indicate that food stamp participation raises adult BMI by a statistically insignificant $0 . 3 \%$ . The literature on food assistance programs and obesity defies easy summary. Results differ by method, sex, and grade. One consistent finding, however, is that the SBP is more protective against obesity than the NSLP, which is consistent with other studies that have found that school breakfasts tend to comply with statutory limits on saturated fat while school lunches tend to exceed them, and that skipping breakfast is associated with higher overall calorie consumption (e.g. Millimet et al., 2010; Morgan et al., 1986). The aforementioned studies seek to identify a point estimate of the causal effect. A different approach is taken by Gundersen et al. (2012) and Kreider et al. (2012), who estimate bounds on the treatment effect of NSLP and SNAP, respectively, using partial identification methods that address the problems of endogenous selection into participation and the underreporting of participation. Their results suggest that the NSLP and SNAP are protective against youth obesity. Utilizing three control groups (children whose household income exceeds the eligibility threshold; incomeeligible children enrolled in schools that do not participate in NSLP, which are largely private schools; and income-eligible children who have dropped out of school), and employing different assumptions about selection and measurement error, Gundersen et al. (2012) estimate that the NSLP reduces obesity by at least $3 . 2 \%$ points or $1 7 \%$ . Kreider et al. (2012) estimate that SNAP reduces the prevalence of youth obesity by at least $5 . 3 \%$ points. 2.3. Income In general, there is a robust negative correlation between weight and income among women but not men; i.e. higher-income women are less likely to be obese (Sobal and Stunkard, 1989; McLaren, 2007). For example, in the NHANES data for 2005–2008, the prevalence of obesity among adult women was $2 9 . 0 \%$ for women living in a household with a poverty-to-income ratio (PIR) greater than $3 5 0 \%$ but $4 2 . 0 \%$ for those living in a household with a PIR of less than $1 3 0 \%$ (Ogden et al., 2010). Research in economics has sought to determine the causal impact of income on weight. In theory, additional income could either increase or decrease weight. Income could lead to weight gain if food and sedentary pursuits are normal goods. However, good health and appearance could also be normal goods, leading one to invest more time and money in slimness and fitness as income rises. The impact of income on weight may follow an inverted U-shape; the first few thousand dollars may be spent heavily on food and thus may increase weight, but at some point the marginal utility of food may decline to the point that additional income results in little increase in calorie consumption; instead, the additional income may be invested in weight loss for the sake of appearance and health (Philipson and Posner, 2003; Lakdawalla et al., 2005). Researchers have exploited natural experiments to study the impact of income on several relevant outcomes, including weight, calorie intake, and food expenditures. A variety of papers have examined the impact of income shocks on weight for specific groups. In general, they tend to find small or no effects of income on weight. For example, Schmeiser (2009) takes advantage of a significant expansion in the Earned Income Tax Credit during the 1990s and uses variation across states and over time in the generosity of the maximum EITC benefit as an instrument for income among families eligible for the EITC. He cannot reject the null hypothesis of no effect of income on weight for men, but finds a modest but statistically significant effect for women, for whom an additional $\$ 1000$ of income per year was associated with an increase in weight of roughly one pound. Akee et al. (2013) estimate the impact of income on adolescent weight using payments made by the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians to their members in western North Carolina. Every six months, the tribe pays a share of casino profits to each member; the payments have averaged $\$ 4000$ per year, are tax free, and raise income by an average of $4 0 \%$ in households with two tribal members. The authors use two control groups: a pure control group of nearby non-tribal members, and a partial control group of adolescent tribal members whose households received the benefit for only two years instead of six during adolescence (the payments began in 1996). The authors find evidence of the non-linearity of weight in income; the payments increase BMI among adolescents from low-income households but have no impact on weight for adolescents in higher-income households. Cawley et al. (2010) estimate the effect of income on weight among the elderly, exploiting the natural experiment of the Social Security Benefits Notch, which was a legislative accident that created substantial unanticipated increases in retirement benefits (averaging roughly $\$ 1000$ in each year of retirement) for certain birth year cohorts in the United States. The authors find no statistically significant impact of income on BMI or the probability of obesity for either men or women, and for men they find precisely estimated zero effects. In general, these papers measure a Local Average Treatment Effect among lower-income individuals. Neither the Social Security payments examined by Cawley et al. (2010) nor the casino payments examined by Akee et al. (2013) were means tested, but the affected groups were relatively lower-income; Social Security beneficiaries tend to have lower earned income (though greater wealth) than working-age adults and Native Americans have a lower median income and higher poverty rate than the nation as a whole (U.S. Census Bureau, 2011). The EITC recipients examined by Schmeiser (2009) are unambiguously a low-income group. Weight may be especially responsive to income among lowincome individuals in developing countries. In a conditional income transfer program in Mexico, families spent an average of $7 0 \%$ of the cash transfer on what the authors describe as “better quality calories”: meat, fruits, and vegetables (Fernald et al., 2008a). The estimated impact of the income transfers on weight (measured using variation in payments due to randomized year of program incorporation but also on family demographic structure which may bias the results) differed for adults and children. For adults, a doubling of payments raised the risk of obesity in adults by $4 1 \%$ (Fernald et al., 2008a), whereas for children aged 24–68 months, it lowered the prevalence of overweight by $8 \%$ (Fernald et al., 2008b). The authors are not able to explain this age difference in the income effect, and are not able to observe mechanisms for the effects on weight. Evidence based on natural experiments implies that the impact of income on food expenditures in developed countries is very small.13 Parker et al. (2008) exploit the timing and amount of stimulus payments made to individuals by the U.S. government during the Great Recession and estimate that recipient households increased their expenditures on food by roughly $2 \%$ of the payment in the three months following the payment. Kuhn et al. (2011) examine the effects of winning the Dutch Postcode Lottery. Comparing participants in winning postcodes to participants in nearby non-winning postcodes, the authors find no significant impact of winning on the amount spent on food at home. Monthly expenditures on food away from home were significantly higher for the winners, but the authors note that this was also true a year before winning, so may be driven by unobserved heterogeneity. The literature on the cycle of purchases and consumption around monthly program receipt indicates that there are shortterm income effects on the quantity of food purchased and calories consumed among low-income individuals participating in government transfer programs. Shapiro (2005) finds that, among food stamp recipients, calorie consumption (estimated from dietary recall data) falls by $0 . 4 0 \%$ each day after receipt of food stamps, or by $1 0 { - } 1 5 \%$ over the course of the month. Hastings and Washington (2010) examine scanner data from three supermarkets in Nevada and estimate that the quantity of food purchased by households receiving food stamps or cash welfare benefits declines $3 2 \%$ throughout the month. Other households that are not benefit recipients do not exhibit the same decline during the month. Mastrobuoni and Weinberg (2009) observe similar behavior among Social Security recipients with low retirement savings; such individuals consume $2 4 \%$ fewer calories the week before receiving their Social Security check relative to the week afterward. In contrast, elderly with more retirement savings tend to smooth their consumption. Although this literature is specific to the cyclical nature of calorie intake in response to monthly payments, it suggests that, for low-income individuals, additional income may lead to higher calorie consumption, at least in the short run. Future research should seek to measure the effects of these cycles of consumption on weight, both within the month (which should be modest) and the cumulative effect over time. Cumulatively, the evidence suggests that, among very lowincome individuals in developed countries, additional income leads to greater expenditures on food, higher calorie intake, and slightly higher weight among adults. Among more middle-income individuals in developed countries (and even the average social security recipient), there is generally no detectable impact of income on weight. There is a need for studies of the impact of income on weight for higher-income individuals. 2.4. Education One of the most consistent findings in health economics is that those with higher education tend to be in better health (see, e.g. Grossman, 2006), and obesity is no exception. In the NHANES data for 2005–2008, the prevalence of adult obesity is $2 3 . 4 \%$ for women with a college degree and $4 2 . 1 \%$ for women who are high school dropouts (Ogden et al., 2010). For men, the correlation is weaker; the prevalence of obesity is $2 7 . 4 \%$ for men with a college degree compared to $3 2 . 1 \%$ for men who are high school dropouts (Ibid). Increased schooling may promote healthy weight later in life through a variety of mechanisms, such as greater health information, healthier diets, increased recreational physical activity, higher income, better health insurance, healthier peers, and safer residential neighborhoods that are more conducive to outdoor exercise. On the other hand, occupations that require higher education may be more sedentary. A large number of studies have estimated the impact of education on health in general and weight in particular; see reviews by Lochner (2011) and Cutler and Lleras-Muney (2010). A series of papers have exploited changes in compulsory schooling laws as an instrument for number of years of completed schooling. One of the strongest such papers is Clark and Royer (2013), which exploits a particularly powerful natural experiment: two changes to British compulsory schooling laws that increased minimum school leaving age from 14 to 16, which affected a majority of the relevant age cohort. Using a regression discontinuity approach that exploits the fact that these changes applied to specific month-year birth cohorts but not others, the authors cannot reject the null hypothesis that schooling has no impact on BMI, overweight, or obesity, although in some cases the estimates are substantial (and positive) but imprecise. Brunello et al. (2013) exploit changes in compulsory schooling laws during the 1960s and 1970s that raised the minimum school-leaving age by 1–3 years, pooling data from several European countries (9 for females and 7 for males). The IV models indicate that they cannot reject the null hypothesis of no impact of schooling on BMI for men. However, the IV models for women suggest that years of schooling lowers BMI of females; an increase in schooling of $1 0 \%$ (slightly more than 1 additional year) reduces women’s average BMI by $1 . 8 4 \%$ and the prevalence of obesity by $1 . 8 5 \%$ points $( 1 4 . 8 3 \% )$ . A team of researchers has exploited a series of natural experiments in the German educational system after World War II, and estimated their impact on weight using recent German Microcensus data (which unfortunately do not include highest grade completed but instead the secondary school track completed, from which the authors impute years of schooling). Models estimated using these various instruments all indicate that there is no detectable impact of education on weight for women, but the results for men differ considerably by instrument. Kemptner et al. (2011) uses changes in compulsory schooling laws as an instrument and finds that, for men, an additional year of schooling lowers BMI by 0.3 units and lowers the risk of obesity by $3 . 0 \%$ points. Jürges et al. (2011) use the construction of academically demanding elementary schools as an instrument. For men, the IV model indicates that an additional year of schooling raises the probability of overweight by $1 2 . 3 \%$ points and raises the probability of obesity by $1 3 . 3 \%$ points; both are implausibly large (rather than describing this as evidence that education increases weight, the authors more cautiously describe it as an absence of evidence that education decreases weight). The third paper in this series (Reinhold and Jürges, 2010) uses abolition of secondary school fees as an instrument and cannot reject the null hypothesis of no effect of education on overweight or obesity for men or women. Anderson and Matsa (2011) examines the effect of an additional year of schooling on weight, but what differentiates this paper from the previous ones is that the outcome is weight at the time that the subjects are still in early elementary school instead of weight during adulthood, when the subjects have completed their schooling. The authors estimate regression discontinuity models that exploit the child’s birth date relative to the cutoff date for school entry, and find no significant effect on BMI or the probability of obesity of being a relatively young first-grader instead of a relatively old kindergartener at the same age. There has been considerable interest in the promise of early childhood interventions to improve adult outcomes (e.g. Heckman et al., 2013). An evaluation of one well-known early childhood intervention, the High/Scope Perry Preschool Program, measured the impact of being randomized to the treatment (a two-year program of $2 . 5 \mathrm { h }$ of academic instruction daily) at age 3–4 years on obesity at age 40 (Muennig et al., 2009). It found that the Perry Preschool treatment had no measurable effect on the probability of adult obesity; in fact, the treatment and control groups had an identical obesity prevalence of $2 7 \%$ . An important caveat is that the sample is extremely small $( N = 1 0 3$ ). Another well-known early childhood intervention is the Carolina Abecedarian Project, which consisted of two stages: an early-childhood stage (from birth to age 5) that sought to facilitate development of language and cognitive skills, and a school-age stage (from age 6 through 8 years) that sought to improve math and reading skills. Campbell et al. (2014) found no evidence of any treatment effect on health from the second, school-age stage, and found mixed results for how the first early-childhood stage may have affected obesity. Assignment to the treatment group in the first stage was associated with a substantial reduction in the probability of being overweight throughout childhood for boys, but did not have a significant impact on the probability of being overweight for girls (Campbell et al., 2014). When subjects were in their mid-30s, data was collected from physical examinations that included measuring weight, height, and waist-to-hip ratio (WHR). Point estimates suggested that the treatment was associated with a large reduction in the probability of obesity (defined by either BMI or WHR) for males, but these were not statistically significant. For females, the treatment was associated with a $1 9 . 8 \%$ point $( 2 6 \% )$ lower probability of obesity defined by WHR, which was statistically significant. Oddly, the treatment was associated with a higher probability of obesity defined by BMI, but this was not statistically significant. The estimates tend to be imprecise because the sample is very small; follow-up physical examination data could be collected for only 68 subjects, and that is before dividing the sample by sex. Another important caveat is that both the Perry Preschool Program and Abecedarian treatments had multiple components; Perry Preschool included home visits by teachers, and Abecedarian included health care and nutritional components. Thus, the estimated effects reflect not just the effect of classroom education but the other program elements as well. Two studies have examined the health impact of the Head Start program and concluded that it reduces the risk of youth obesity. Carneiro and Ginja (2014) estimate a fuzzy regression discontinuity model that exploits a number of discontinuities across family size, family structure, state, and year in income eligibility for Head Start. Examining data on boys in the Children of the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth, 1979 Cohort, they find that participating in Head Start between the ages of 3 and 5 years reduces the probability of obesity at ages 12–13 by $2 9 \%$ and has no impact on the probability of obesity at ages 16–17. The effect at ages 12–13 seems to be concentrated among African-American boys. (The authors cannot estimate the impact of the program for girls because there is no jump in the probability of Head Start participation for girls around the income cutoffs.) Frisvold and Lumeng (2011) identify the impact of full-day versus half-day Head Start for youth, exploiting the natural experiment of an unanticipated cancelation, due to statewide budget cuts to education, of a grant that funded full-day Head Start. They examine five years of data from one Head Start program in Michigan that include multiple measurements of weight and height for each child $( N = 1 5 3 2 )$ . Their IV estimates indicate that full-day (compared to half-day) Head Start decreases youth obesity by $1 7 . 6 \%$ points. This may be implausibly large, but Hausman tests indicate that their non-IV model is preferred; that model implies a $4 \%$ point reduction in obesity, which the authors estimate could be explained by a reduction in consumption of 20 calories per day. The results of this research are extremely varied. Overall, it seems that early childhood education (including Head Start) may have protective effects at younger but not necessarily older ages, and that primary and secondary schooling has little if any impact on obesity. Future research should examine whether the overall null effect found in some studies is an average of meaningfully different effects in different subgroups; Cutler et al. (forthcoming) find that the association of education with obesity varies considerably across countries (see Fig. 1D in that paper), which suggests that it may also vary by region, race, and ethnicity. All of the studies discussed in this section measure the effect of preschool, primary or secondary schooling; future research should seek to identify the effect of additional years of college education. 2.5. Macroeconomic conditions The macroeconomy is another possible contributor to obesity. When the unemployment rate is high many people experience declines in income and employment. This decrease in labor market opportunities can have both substitution and income effects. The substitution effect is relatively straightforward: when wages are low so is the opportunity cost of time, and thus recessions may lead to more time-intensive investments in health such as physical activity and cooking from scratch. The income effect on health is ambiguous. Lower income could lead to a decrease in calorie consumption (e.g. cooking rice and beans at home instead of buying fast food) or an increase in calories (e.g. substituting energy-dense, low nutrient foods for more expensive fresh fruits and vegetables). Even conditional on income and employment, economic downturns could affect health by increasing stress, taking up mental bandwidth and reducing self-control or willpower (Mani et al., 2013), with deleterious consequences for diet and physical activity (e.g. De Vriendt et al., 2009). Stress also leads to the release of the hormone cortisol, which has complex effects but can increase appetite (especially for energy-dense foods), insulin resistance, and increased abdominal fat accumulation (e.g. Bjorntorp, 1997). Ruhm (2005) tested whether the state employment rate was associated with excess weight and physical inactivity. Reducedform models were estimated under the assumption that changes in local unemployment rates are exogenous; the models control for state, month, and year fixed effects, and thus identification comes from variation in the employment rate within states over time, relative to the corresponding changes in other states. Results of these models, estimated using data from the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) for 1987–2000, are consistent with Ruhm’s general findings that “good times make you sick” and there is “healthy living in hard times.” In models that exclude employment status and income (and thus allow the effect of the employment rate to operate through changes in those variables), a $1 \%$ point decrease in the employment rate is estimated to reduce the probability of obesity by $0 . 7 3 \%$ points and to decrease the probability of physical inactivity by $0 . 2 1 \%$ points. These results are driven by improvements among the least healthy; morbid obesity and complete inactivity decrease. The results do not operate through changes in employment; in fact, the results are of equal size or larger for the employed population. In earlier work, Ruhm (2000) examined the BRFSS for 1987–1995 and found that a $1 \%$ point increase in the state unemployment rate was associated with a $2 \%$ decrease in daily fat intake, but no statistically significant change in daily servings of fruits and vegetables.
