Ruhm (2005) cautions that these results are specific to temporary macroeconomic fluctuations and do not imply that long-run economic growth worsens weight and exercise. In contrast to Ruhm’s findings that weight-related health is counter-cyclical, Charles and DeCicca (2008) find evidence that it is procyclical, with this relationship concentrated among the economically vulnerable. Because they examine MSA-level unemployment rates instead of state-level employment rates, they have to exclude those living outside of large MSAs from their sample of men in the National Health Interview Survey for 1997–2001. Estimating models by race, they find that a $1 \%$ point increase in the unemployment rate leads to a $2 . 2 \%$ point increase in the probability of obesity for African-American men, with smaller and statistically insignificant changes in the probability of obesity for Hispanic and White men. Estimating models based on the predicted probability that the respondent was employed, they find that those least likely to be employed experience the greatest increases in weight when the unemployment rate rises. They explore possible mechanisms and find no consistent link between the unemployment rate and exercise. Noting that their results are concentrated among low-SES individuals who may be at greatest risk from macroeconomic downturns, they hypothesize that their results are due to the biological effects of stress, such as stress-related eating, and elevated levels of cortisol promoting the accumulation of body fat. Other evidence on mechanisms comes from Dave and Kelly (2012), who find robust evidence in the BRFSS for 1990–2009 that a higher unemployment rate is associated with reduced consumption of fruits and vegetables, with weaker evidence of substitution toward snacks and fast food. Arkes (2009) studies the impact of the macroeconomy on the weight of young adults (aged 15–18 years) in the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth, 1997 Cohort, for 1997–2004. Arkes (2009) estimates models similar to those of Ruhm (2000) and finds that male teenagers gain weight in strong macroeconomic times, but female teenagers do the opposite – they gain weight during macroeconomic downturns. A $1 \%$ point increase in the state unemployment rate is associated with a $1 . 3 \%$ point lower probability that a teenage boy is overweight and a $1 . 8 \%$ point higher probability that a teenage girl is overweight.14 One important mechanism by which macroeconomic conditions may affect the weight of adults is through job loss. Deb et al. (2011) identify the impact of job loss using respondent reports of whether they lost their job because the business closed; the rationale is that a firm shutdown is more exogenously determined than the job separation of individuals. They utilize data on middle-aged and elderly Americans in the Health and Retirement Study, 1992–2008. Speculating that there may be important heterogeneity in people’s response to job loss, they estimate a finite mixture model. They find that the first latent component $84 \%$ of the sample) had small but statistically insignificant decreases in BMI, but the second latent component ( $1 6 \%$ of the sample) had large and statistically significant increases in BMI, after business closure. In this second group, job loss resulted in a gain of one BMI unit, or roughly 7 pounds for a man of average height. People in this second, more affected, component differed from those in the first in that they were $2 2 \%$ more likely to be obese, and were more likely to be female, lower-income, less educated, and middle-aged rather than elderly. These results are consistent with those of Charles and DeCicca (2008); the economically vulnerable appear to be most affected by the macroeconomy and job loss. In summary, there appears to be considerable heterogeneity across age, gender, urbanicity, and socioeconomic status in the effect of the macroeconomy on diet, physical activity, and weight. It is unclear the extent to which these differing results are a result of studies using different methods and datasets and examining different time periods; future research could seek to estimate consistent models in a single dataset for various subgroups. Although the results are quite divergent, the fact that the unemployment rate has repeatedly been associated with diet, physical activity, and weight should make researchers cautious about using unemployment rate as an instrument for other possible causes of obesity. For example, unemployment rate has been used as an instrument for maternal employment in a model of child obesity (e.g. Anderson et al., 2003), but this may be invalid because the unemployment rate may have a direct impact on child weight and thus be correlated with the second-stage error term in the IV model. 2.6. Peer and neighborhood effects Peers may influence diet or physical activity through bandwagon effects; it may be more enjoyable to eat, diet, or exercise when one’s peers are doing the same. Identifying peer effects is notoriously difficult because individuals tend to associate with people like themselves and peers tend to have similar environmental influences (Manski, 1993). Yakusheva et al. (2014) identify peer effects by exploiting the randomization of freshman roommates at two universities. Following the literature that defines the roommate receiving influence as the ego and the roommate doing the influencing as the alter, they estimate the influence of the alter’s weight at baseline (just before freshman year) on the change in weight of the ego during freshman year; the model also controls for a complete set of indicator variables for all possible combinations of the factors used by the administration to make roommate assignments (such as preferred area of campus and smoking status). Results from these models are consistent with a significant positive peer effect on weight for females; for every standard deviation increase in the baseline weight of the alter, the ego gains an additional 0.8 pounds during freshman year (compared to an average freshman year weight gain of 2.4 pounds). They cannot reject the null hypothesis of no peer effects on weight for males. The authors explore heterogeneity in these peer effects, and find that the females who are most influenced by their roommates are those in the lowest and highest quartiles of the baseline weight distribution. They also find that alters have the greatest effect on egos when the alter is higher in the social hierarchy; specifically, when the alter is lighter, comes from a higher-SES household, or is more sexually experienced than the ego. There are no such differences for males. A major social experiment found strong evidence of neighborhood effects, which may in part reflect the impact of a new set of peers. Kling et al. (2007) and Ludwig et al. (2011) examine the effect of the Moving to Opportunity program on weight. From 1994 to 1998, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development randomized nearly 4500 women with children who were living in public housing in high-poverty urban census tracts in five major U.S. cities to one of three groups: one received housing vouchers that were redeemable only if they moved to a low-poverty census tract, a second received the unrestricted traditional Section 8 housing vouchers and a third received neither of these opportunities. In 2002, an average of 5 years after random assignment, the researchers collected data on self-reported weight. For adults, the effect of Intention to Treat was that the group offered the lowpoverty vouchers was $4 . 8 \%$ points less likely to be obese than the control group; assuming that there was no effect on those who did not use the voucher to move, the effect of Treatment on the Treated was a $1 0 . 3 \%$ point reduction in the probability of obesity (Kling et al., 2007). The researchers conducted another follow-up in 2008–2010, an average of 12.6 years after randomization, and this time measured the respondents’ weight, height, and tested their blood for diabetes. Ludwig et al. (2011) estimate that the effect of Intention to Treat was that the group offered low-poverty vouchers were $4 . 6 1 \%$ points $( 1 3 . 0 \% )$ less likely to have a $\mathsf { B M I } \geq 3 5 , 3 . 3 8 \%$ points $( 1 9 . 1 \% )$ less likely to have a ${ \mathrm { B M I } } \geq 4 0$ , and were $4 . 3 1 \%$ points $( 2 1 . 6 \% )$ less likely to have diabetes. The small difference in the probability of overall obesity $\left( \mathsf { B M I } \geq 3 0 \right)$ was not statistically significant. The group randomized to the traditional Section 8 voucher program was less likely than the control group to have a $\mathsf { B M I } \geq 3 5$ but the other differences between the Section 8 treatment group and the control group were not statistically significant. Thus, it seems that the requirement to move to a low-income neighborhood was important for the beneficial effect on weight. Some of these studies were able to investigate the mechanisms by which these peer and neighborhood effects operate. Kling et al. (2007) attribute the lower rate of obesity among movers to increases in exercise and improvements in nutrition (which could be the result of new peers or a lower time cost of shopping for healthy food). Yakusheva et al. (2014) test for peer effects on self-reported exercise frequency and eating disorders but find little evidence of any. Carrell et al. (2011) exploits the randomized assignment of students at the U.S. Air Force Academy to squadrons (groups of 30 with whom cadets spend most of their time) to test whether being assigned to a squadron of alters who were less fit during high school affects two important outcomes: the cadet’s physical education score that semester and whether the cadet failed the Academy’s physical fitness requirements. Using a sample that is unusually large for this topic (over 13,000), they regress the ego’s outcomes on the average high school fitness scores of the rest of the squadron (the alters). The results indicate that a one standard deviation increase in the high school fitness scores of all peers in the group raises the ego’s college fitness score by 0.165 of a standard deviation; this is large – roughly $4 0 \%$ as strong as the effect of the ego’s own high school fitness. A one standard deviation increase in the high school fitness scores of all peers in the group also lowers the probability that the ego fails the college fitness test by $4 . 7 \%$ points; this is even larger, approximately $7 0 \%$ as strong as the effect of the ego’s own high school fitness. In other models they find that the most influential alters, and the most influenced egos, are those who are least fit. However, before generalizing from this finding one should keep in mind that cadets at the U.S. Air Force Academy are specifically selected to be fit, so the least fit in that group are still above the population average. Overall, there is evidence of peer and neighborhood effects on weight for women and on fitness for men. An important priority is to better explain this gender differences in peer effects, identify peer effects for other peer groups of interest, such as coworkers, and how it varies over the life cycle (e.g. do peer effects on weight among women peak during the teenage years?). It would be useful to know whether eating disorders such as anorexia nervosa and bulimia can spread through female networks in high school and college (such as sororities and sports and cheerleading teams), although this likely faces the additional challenges of a high degree of misreporting and a relatively uncommon outcome. It is also a priority to determine how to harness the positive influence of peer effects to increase retention and improve outcomes in exercise, diet and weight loss programs. 3. The economic consequences of obesity The economic consequences of obesity include worse labor market outcomes, such as lower wages and a lower probability of employment, and higher medical care costs. When studying the causes of obesity, there is often the potential to conduct randomized experiments: e.g. to randomize children into a preschool program in order to measure the impact of education on obesity or to randomize college roommates in order to test for peer effects in weight. That is more difficult when obesity is the endogenous regressor rather than the outcome. It would, obviously, be unethical to force a subject randomized to the treatment group to become obese so one could study the resulting increase in medical care costs. It is possible to randomly assign overweight individuals interested in weight loss to a weight loss treatment, but the effect measured would reflect not just the weight change but also the method of achieving it (such as bariatric surgery or increased time spent physically active) which could have a direct impact on the outcome. Due to the challenges of experimentally manipulating individuals’ weights, the literature on the economic consequences of obesity has relied solely on natural experiments for identification. In contrast to the research on the economic causes of obesity, which was often characterized by conflicting results, the evidence on the economic consequences of obesity is relatively consistent: obesity worsens labor market outcomes and raises medical care costs. One interesting aspect of this literature is that the medical definition of obesity (a BMI of 30 or higher) does not coincide with the economic consequences of obesity; wages for women begin falling with BMI in the healthy weight range (Kline and Tobias, 2008; Gregory and Ruhm, 2011) while medical care costs do not rise significantly with BMI until the morbidly obese range (Cawley et al., 2015). 3.1. Wages A large literature has estimated the effect of weight or obesity on wages (see Averett, 2011, for a review). Cawley (2004) exploits the heritable component of weight by using the BMI of an adult biological sibling as an instrument for the BMI of the respondent. This instrument has the advantage of being powerful; twin studies indicate very high levels of heritability for BMI, up to $7 0 \mathrm { - } 8 0 \%$ (Farooqi and O’Rahilly, 2007; Pietilainen, 2014). The potential threat to validity is that the genes that affect obesity may also affect other things correlated with the error term in the wage equation. One might also be concerned about the possibility that a shared household environment makes biological relatives similar in weight and could be correlated with outcomes, but the preponderance of evidence suggests that any shared household environment effect on weight is so small as to be undetectable (see the review in Cawley and Meyerhoefer, 2012); consistent with this, the weight of nonbiological relatives (e.g. stepchildren or adopted children) are not significant predictors of respondent weight in the first stage of IV (Cawley, 2004; Lindeboom et al., 2010; Cawley and Meyerhoefer, 2012). Estimating IV models using data from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth, 1979 Cohort, for 1981–2000, Cawley (2004) finds that the effect of weight on wages varies by race and gender, with the greatest impact on white females, for whom an additional 10 pounds lowers wages by $2 . 8 \%$ . Several other studies have applied this IV method to samples for other countries. For example, Brunello and D’Hombres (2007) apply the method to data for nine countries in the European Community Household Panel; their IV models indicate that weight lowers wages for women in Italy, Portugal and Finland, and for men in Italy, Spain, Austria, and Ireland; some of the null results may be due to the very small samples in each country (485–5355). When they pool the data on all nine countries, their IV models indicate that a $1 0 \%$ increase in BMI reduces the wages of females by $1 . 8 6 \%$ and males by $3 . 2 7 \%$ . To test for non-linearities in these effects, Kline and Tobias (2008) allow BMI to enter the IV wage equation non-parametrically and instrument for respondent weight using the weight of a biological parent. Using data from the 1970 British Cohort Study, they estimate that BMI lowers the wages of women along the entire range of BMI, but the decrease is steepest in the range of approximately BMI 20–28. They also find that BMI lowers wages for men, and in a relatively linear fashion. In summary, there is evidence that weight lowers wages in economically developed countries. Studies have found this effect for both women and men, but the magnitude of the effects differs by gender and race. For example, in the U.S. the obesity wage penalty is greater for women than men and greater for white females than African-American or Hispanic females (Cawley, 2004). Future research should examine the extent to which these wage gaps are due to discrimination, job absenteeism and lower productivity on the job; I return to this topic in the later section on the externalities associated with obesity. 3.2. Employment Others have examined the effect of obesity on employment. Lindeboom et al. (2010) examine data from the British National Child Development Study, which consists of 17,000 individuals born in Great Britain in one week in 1958, and records employment at ages 33 and 42 years. They observe large differences in the probability of employment between obese and non-obese men and women, but when they estimate IV models that use parental obesity status as an instrument for respondent weight, they cannot reject the null hypothesis that obesity has no effect on employment. Another study to test for an impact of obesity on employment in the UK (Morris, 2007) instrumented for respondent obesity using the prevalence of obesity in the local health authority, but this may be invalid if respondents sort into neighborhoods based on unobserved demand (e.g. for proximity to restaurants or exercise opportunities). Although it is difficult to experimentally manipulate individuals’ weights, one clever study devised a way to experimentally manipulate employer’s perceptions of job applicants’ weights. Rooth (2009) tested for discrimination against obese job applicants by submitting fictitious job applications to 989 real job openings in urban Sweden. The applications were sent in pairs, with resumes created to be as identical as possible without arousing employer suspicion. Each of the applications included a photo of the applicant, which is a common practice in Sweden. The paired applicants were chosen to be as identical as possible (with respect to hair color, hair length, smile, and overall attractiveness), but the photo for one of the two was manipulated using computer software to make the individual appear obese. The study estimates that the obese applicant was significantly less likely to be contacted for a job interview than the other member of the pair; this disadvantage equaled $8 \%$ points for women and $6 \%$ points for men. The disadvantage was similar across occupation for men, but it varied across occupation for women: $2 1 \%$ points for those applying to be restaurant workers, $1 5 \%$ points for those applying to be accountants and $7 \%$ points for those applying to be preschool teachers, but no significant difference for applications to be computer specialists or nurses. When the author controls for a third-party rating of the attractiveness of the photograph, he finds that employer discrimination is on the basis of obesity for female applicants and on the basis of attractiveness for male applicants. A large number of laboratory studies that ask subjects to make hypothetical decisions about hiring, compensation and promotions also find consistent evidence of discrimination against obese workers and applicants (see, e.g. Roehling et al., 2013). 3.3. Medical care costs Given the strong link between obesity and heart disease, cancer, and Type II diabetes, another likely economic consequence of obesity is elevated medical care costs. Cawley and Meyerhoefer (2012) and Cawley et al. (2015) estimate IV two-part models of medical expenditures using data from the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey. The IV model exploits the heritable component of weight by instrumenting for respondent obesity using the BMI and BMI squared of a biological child. The models indicate that in 2010 obesity raised annual medical care costs by $\$ 3508$ (in 2010 dollars); however, the effects of BMI on medical care costs are highly non-linear (Cawley et al., 2015). For men, medical care costs are Ushaped in BMI, with much higher expenditures for those who are underweight or morbidly obese. For women, medical care costs are J-shaped in BMI with a large increase in medical care costs with BMI among those who are morbidly obese. For both men and women, predicted medical care costs for individuals just over the threshold of obesity are not significantly higher than those of healthy weight individuals. However, costs rise exponentially in the morbidly obese range $\left( \mathsf { B M I } \ge 3 5 \right)$ , which indicates that the greatest potential savings may come from facilitating weight loss in that group or preventing additional weight gain among obese individuals. This pattern of medical care expenditures matches that of mortality risk: flat throughout the overweight and obese class 1 range, rising with BMI in the morbidly obese range; see Flegal et al. (2013). Assuming that the estimates from the regression sample of adults with biological children in the household generalize to the full population of non-institutionalized adults, the IV model implies that the total direct medical care costs of obesity for the U.S. population of adults was $\$ 315.8$ billion in 2010, which equaled $2 7 . 5 \%$ of the health expenditures for non-institutionalized U.S. adults (Cawley et al., 2015). 4. The negative externalities of obesity Obesity imposes large external costs, which likely decrease social welfare. Third-party payers cover most of the costs of obesity related illness; e.g. in 2005, $8 8 . 2 \%$ of the total medical care costs of obesity in the U.S. were paid by health insurance companies, Medicare, and Medicaid (Cawley and Meyerhoefer, 2012). Ultimately, many of these costs of obesity were paid by non-obese individuals. In group health insurance, the premium paid by each individual does not depend upon his or her weight; as a result, healthy-weight individuals subsidize the health care costs of obese individuals. The same is true for Medicare, which is funded by payroll taxes, and Medicaid, which is funded with general revenues; in public health insurance programs, healthy-weight individuals subsidize the medical care costs of obese individuals. No one has challenged that obesity imposes negative externalities through public health insurance. However, the extent of externalities in employer-provided group health insurance has been questioned; Bhattacharya and Bundorf (2009) argue that obese workers with employer-provided health insurance pay for their higher health care costs in the form of lower wages. However, if wage penalties existed to internalize medical care costs, then they should be negligible until the morbidly obese range (Cawley et al., 2015). In fact, women’s wages fall with BMI along the entire range of BMI and the marginal effect of BMI on wages is largest in the healthy weight range (Kline and Tobias, 2008), where medical care costs are flat over BMI (see Cawley and Meyerhoefer, 2012, Fig. 3). Gregory and Ruhm (2011) estimate flexible IV models of weight and wages in which sibling BMI is an instrument for the BMI of the respondent, using the Panel Survey of Income Dynamics, and conclude that women’s wages peak at a BMI of roughly 23, far below the threshold of obesity or even overweight, which they interpret as evidence against the theory of Bhattacharya and Bundorf (2009); instead, they conclude that wages fall with BMI because employers have preferences for appearance. A large number of studies document employer discrimination on the basis of weight; see Puhl (2011) for a review. In addition, obese individuals earn less in many countries of the world that have universal public health insurance, such as Austria, Denmark, England, Finland, France, Germany, Italy, and Sweden (see e.g. Caliendo and Gehrsitz, 2014; Averett, 2011; Brunello and D’Hombres, 2007). In such countries employers do not provide health insurance and thus they have no incentive or even ability to internalize the external medical care costs of obesity. Overall, it seems more likely that the obesity wage penalty is due to employer discrimination or lower productivity than an attempt by employers to internalize the external health care costs of obesity. Health care cost externalities of obesity can lead to deadweight loss in two ways (Bhattacharya and Sood, 2011, 2007). First, externalities raise average premiums in the private health insurance market, which results in lower take-up and suboptimal amounts of coverage.15 In public health insurance, the higher medical care costs are passed on to the public in the form of higher payroll taxes (for Medicare) and income taxes (for Medicaid), which leads to decreased labor supply.16 Thus, the external costs of obesity in health insurance distort decisions in both health insurance markets and labor markets, imposing deadweight loss. The second potential source of deadweight loss arises because of moral hazard; individuals who do not pay the full medical care costs of excess weight may underinvest in a healthy diet, physical activity, weight loss or prevention of weight gain (Bhattacharya and Sood, 2007). Several studies have examined the effects of increasing health insurance coverage at the extensive or intensive margin, but it is difficult to infer much from this about moral hazard because increased insurance, by increasing consumption of health care, may have a direct effect on BMI. Several studies examine the extensive margin of health insurance. Dave and Kaestner (2009) examine changes in health behaviors among those who newly qualify for Medicare and find evidence consistent with moral hazard: controlling for employment status and number of doctor visits, gaining Medicare coverage is associated with a $1 5 . 1 \%$ point $( 4 0 \% )$ decrease in the probability that men engage in vigorous physical exercise. Other studies examine the impact on obesity as opposed to diet and physical activity. A randomized experiment found that providing Medicaid to Oregon residents had no statistically significant impact on the probability of obesity, although the confidence intervals were very wide (Baicker et al., 2013). In contrast, two studies that exploit state Medicaid expansions as natural experiments find evidence that health insurance coverage raises BMI (Kelly and Markowitz, 2009/2010; Bhattacharya et al., 2011). With respect to the intensive margin of insurance, Bhattacharya et al. (2011) examined historic data from the RAND health insurance experiment and found no evidence that the generosity of insurance raises BMI. Overall, the health insurance externality of obesity is likely to impose deadweight loss by reducing purchases of health insurance and reducing labor supply, and less likely to greatly distort decisions about diet, physical activity, and weight loss. Calculating the extent of such deadweight loss would be a useful direction for future research. 5. Policies to internalize the external costs of obesity There are several possible approaches to internalizing the external costs of obesity. The most direct would be to tax excess body fat by an amount equal to its marginal external cost. No country has yet implemented such a tax, perhaps because of concerns about discriminating against those with a genetic predisposition to fatness. However, Singapore implemented a program called “Trim and Fit” from 1992 to 2008 in which schoolchildren’s BMIs were measured and youths deemed overweight were assigned extra physical activity at school. There were no financial penalties for youths or their families but schools could be rewarded or punished based on progress toward goals. Singapore’s health ministry reported that the prevalence of youth obesity declined as a result (Toh et al., 2002) but it is not clear whether the intervention was rigorously evaluated. Japan in 2008 passed what was nicknamed the ‘metabo law’ (after the metabolic syndrome, a set of risk factors for heart disease that includes a large waist circumference) that requires companies and local governments to add to the mandatory checkups for adults aged 40–75 a measurement of waist circumference; individuals who exceed the limits (33.5 in. for men and 35.4 in. for women) are counseled on dieting and weight loss. There are no financial penalties for individuals but employers and local governments face fines for failing to meet targets. Most policies and programs that could be used to internalize the external costs of obesity do not levy taxes or penalties directly on fatness or weight. Instead, they take the form of: raising health insurance premia for obese individuals, offering financial rewards for weight loss, taxing foods that are energy-dense, subsidizing foods that are nutritious and less energy dense, and subsidizing physical activity. These programs are discussed in the following sections. 5.3. Taxes on energy-dense foods Financial rewards for weight loss have a mixed record of effectiveness (Cawley and Price, 2013; Department of the Treasury, Department of Labor, and Department of Health and Human Services, 2013; Horwitz et al., 2013; Jeffery, 2012). Some studies have found substantial weight loss in such programs. For example, Volpp et al. (2008) find that offering a lottery with an expected daily value of \$3 results in an average weight loss of 9.2 pounds relative to the control group after 16 weeks. In contrast, several studies have found no detectable weight loss from rewards that consisted of: $\$ 7-14$ per percentage point of weight lost (Finkelstein et al., 2007), $\$ 100$ per month for achieving weight loss goals (Kullgren et al., 2013), or $\$ 3-5$ per quarter for each percentage point of baseline weight lost (Cawley and Price, 2013). An important limitation of this research is that the participants are volunteers interested in weight loss; thus, it is unknown how effective incentives would be for people who do not wish to lose weight (Jeffery, 2012). Another complication is that attrition in such programs can be substantial, despite the fact that all participants are volunteers being paid to achieve their own goals; e.g. the workplace wellness program studied by Cawley and Price (2013) experienced attrition of $5 4 . 9 \%$ after 3 months and $7 5 . 8 \%$ after 12 months. Clearly, behavior change and attrition in such programs is partly a function of the way in which the incentives are designed (Volpp et al., 2011). In general, incentives are more effective when they are immediate, salient, and take advantage of loss aversion, mental accounting, and risk preferences (see, e.g. Ainslie, 1975; Volpp et al., 2011). An important research priority is to determine the optimal design of incentives for weight loss and related behavior change. Others have sought to incentivize exercise rather than weight. Royer et al. (forthcoming) conducted a randomized experiment at a Fortune 500 company in which the treatment group was offered $\$ 10$ per visit to the company gym for up to 3 visits per week for four weeks and find that the treatment doubled gym attendance. Charness and Gneezy (2009) find that offering university students $\$ 100$ to visit the gym at least eight times in four weeks more than doubles their weekly gym visits relative to a control group. Florida offered incentives for Medicaid enrollees to participate in exercise programs. Although the program was not formally evaluated, only two participants of the 428,000 who were automatically enrolled earned credits for participating in exercise programs; researchers have speculated that the incentives were too small, not salient, and that participants had insufficient knowledge of the program (Blumenthal et al., 2013). One concern about such incentive schemes is that the provision of external incentives may crowd out intrinsic motivation; the worst case scenario is that after the external incentives end, individuals are less motivated and health behaviors are worse than before the intervention. Studies of incentives for exercise find that exercise remains somewhat elevated after the removal of incentives (Royer et al., forthcoming; Charness and Gneezy, 2009). Likewise, studies have documented substantial weight regain after financial incentives for weight loss ended (e.g. Cawley and Price, 2013; Jeffery, 2012; John et al., 2011) but participants do not end up heavier than they were before the intervention. Thus, external incentives do not appear to crowd out intrinsic motivation for exercise or weight loss. Perhaps the anti-obesity policy that has been most commonly proposed (e.g. Kamerow, 2010; Brownell and Frieden, 2009; Brownell et al., 2009) and most heavily studied by economists is a tax on energy-dense, low-nutrient foods such as sugar-sweetened beverages (SSB). In the U.S., 34 states tax soft drinks sold in grocery stores, at an average rate of $4 . 0 2 \%$ , and 15 states tax snacks sold in grocery stores at an average rate of $1 . 2 \%$ (Chriqui et al., 2008). Numerous countries have recently taxed energy-dense, non-nutritious foods, such as Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Hungary, Norway, and Mexico. Such taxes have practical challenges. It is unclear what set of foods should be taxed; there is no specific subset of foods that cause obesity, and the risk of taxing a small number of foods is that consumers may switch to energy-dense items that are untaxed (Chouinard et al., 2007; Fletcher et al., 2010a, 2013; Zhen et al., 2014). Another challenge is that when taxes are enacted by geographically small jurisdictions they can be evaded through cross-border shopping (Tosun and Skidmore, 2007). There is also concern that food taxes are regressive. However, several states both tax food and in general provide tax credits to low-income households, which allows for the substitution effect, but eliminates the income effect, of the tax (Cawley, 2012). Numerous studies have documented consumer responses to changes in food taxes. For example, Fletcher et al. (2010a,b) estimate models that control for state and year fixed effects using data on adults from the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System for 1990–2006 (when 28 states changed their tax rates on SSBs), and on youths from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Surveys for 1989–2006. For youths, they estimate that a $1 \%$ point increase in the tax on SSBs (relative to a mean of $2 . 7 \%$ ) decreases youth soft drink consumption by just 6 calories per day. However, that decreased consumption of SSBs is offset by increased consumption of milk, with the result that there is no significant change in total calories consumed. Not surprisingly, there is no detectable effect of SSB taxes on youth weight (Fletcher et al., 2010a). For adults, they find statistically significant but extremely small impacts of SSB taxes on weight; a $1 \%$ point (or nearly $5 0 \%$ ) increase in the state tax rate on SSBs leads to a decrease in BMI of 0.003 units and a decrease in obesity of $0 . 0 1 \%$ points (Fletcher et al., 2010b). A challenge for predicting the impact of large taxes on energydense foods is that they do not currently exist in the U.S. so it requires projecting out of sample. Some have sought to estimate the impact of larger taxes using elasticities of demand calculated using naturally occurring variation in food prices; a limitation of this is that the naturally occurring variation may be endogenous – due in part to differences in demand across areas or changes in demand over time within areas – resulting in biased estimates of elasticities. Finkelstein et al. (2013) simulate the effect of a $2 0 \%$ tax on SSBs, using Nielsen Homescan data and allowing for potential substitutions between SSBs and 19 categories of other types of food. They estimate two-stage residual inclusion IV models that address the endogeneity of prices by instrumenting for the household price index of each food category using the weighted average of the price indices of all other households in the same market excluding those in the same census tract; this assumes that all demand shocks are limited to the census tract, and are not common to the broader market. They estimate that a $2 0 \%$ price increase on SSBs would lead to very little substitution to other categories of energy-dense food and would reduce the purchases of calories from stores by $4 . 7 \%$ , which they estimate would result in a weight loss of 1.6 pounds in the first year and 2.9 pounds over 10 years. This paper examines 19 categories of food rather than the universe of groceries; a subsequent paper by the same authors that examines a broader set of foods that represented about half of all at-home caloric intake (and used a different functional form) found evidence of greater substitution away from SSBs and toward other food categories (Zhen et al., 2014). As a result, the estimated impact on weight of the $2 0 \%$ tax on SSBs was less: a reduction of 0.8 lbs for low-income individuals and 0.4 lbs for high-income individuals after one year, and a reduction of 1.5 lbs for low-income individuals and 0.7 lbs for high-income individuals after 10 years. Limitations of both studies are that they observe purchases, not consumption, they use data on half or less of calories consumed from groceries, and they do not observe food purchases from vending machines or restaurants. The model in Finkelstein et al. (2013) also does not allow for income effects from the taxes. A substantial number of studies have experimentally manipulated food prices, sometimes by very large amounts; however, these tend to lower the price of healthier foods rather than dramatically raise the price of energy-dense foods (Epstein et al., 2012). In general, it is difficult to experimentally simulate a tax in the field because people can avoid it by shopping elsewhere. Overall, the evidence suggests that taxes on energy-dense foods would probably have to be much higher than their current rates to have a meaningful impact on consumption (Fletcher et al., forthcoming, 2011; Chaloupka et al., 2011; Powell and Chaloupka, 2009), and even then if taxes are narrowly applied then substitution to untaxed items may result, which would limit the effect on weight (Fletcher et al., 2013; Schroeter et al., 2008; Chouinard et al., 2007; Zhen et al., 2014). 5.4. Subsidies for healthy food An alternative to taxing energy-dense, non-nutritious foods is to subsidize nutritious, less energy-dense foods. A large number of studies have experimentally subsidized the prices of healthy foods, sometimes by very large amounts; see the review in Epstein et al. (2012). Some take place in laboratory settings with questionable generalizability, but others have taken place in cafeterias or vending machines in the field. For example, subsidizing fruit and salads in university and high school cafeterias by $5 0 \%$ resulted in a tripling to quadrupling of sales (Jeffery et al., 1994; French et al., 1997); however, these price reductions were combined with other interventions such as signs and increased diversity of healthy food choices, so that increase in demand cannot be attributed solely to the price change. Moreover, the behavior change did not result in lasting healthier habits; sales fell back to baseline levels after the removal of the subsidy. More recently, Ni Mhurchu et al. (2010) conducted a randomized experiment to estimate the impact of a $1 2 . 5 \%$ discount on the price of healthier foods on grocery purchases. It was conducted in New Zealand with 1104 shoppers from one retail supermarket chain, and food and beverages were classified as healthier or less healthy using nutrition recommendations from the Heart Foundation. Purchases were tracked using supermarket electronic scanners. At six months, the impact of the discount on purchases of saturated fat, total fat, and sugars were small and statistically insignificant, but the treatment was associated with an $1 1 \%$ increase in purchases of healthier foods, which amounted to an additional $0 . 7 9 \mathrm { k g }$ per week, including $0 . 4 8 \mathrm { k g / w k }$ more fruit and vegetables. This may be an underestimate of the true price effect because the price change was not very salient: prices on supermarket shelves were not altered; instead, treatment group members were mailed a list of foods that were discounted. There is weak evidence that some of the increase in sales persisted 6 months after the discount ended. The USDA recently conducted a pilot test of a Healthy Incentives Program in SNAP that offered a $3 0 \%$ rebate on each dollar of SNAP benefits spent on targeted fruits and vegetables (they could be fresh, canned, frozen, or dried but without added sugar or fat; white potatoes and fruit juice were also excluded). The rebate was credited to the SNAP Electronic Benefit Transfer card for a maximum of $\$ 60$ per month, a cap that few households reached. The rebate could be spent on any SNAP-eligible groceries. A randomized controlled experiment involving 55,000 households indicated that the incentives increased consumption of fresh fruits and vegetables by $2 5 \%$ , which equaled 0.22 cups or roughly 3.5 tablespoons per day (USDA, 2013). While studies have demonstrated that subsidizing healthy foods can lead to increased purchases of those foods, they have not been shown to reduce obesity. That is, there is not yet evidence that the increased consumption of nutritious food leads to a decrease in the consumption of energy-dense, non-nutritious food sufficient to reduce weight. The risk is that such subsidies may increase overall calorie intake, further increasing weights. There may be health benefits from improved nutrition, however. 5.5. Subsidies for physical activity Taxpayers subsidize the physical activity of youth through sports teams and physical education (PE) classes in public schools. Several organizations, such as the Centers for Disease Control, American Academy of Pediatrics, and Institute of Medicine, have called for increases in PE to prevent and reduce youth obesity. To estimate the impact of PE on the physical activity and weight of high school students, Cawley et al. (2007) instrument for the amount of time that high school students spend in PE using state PE requirements, while controlling for state socioeconomic characteristics and education spending to reduce the risks of policy endogeneity. IV models, estimated using data from the Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System, indicate that increasing PE time increases physical activity among high school girls (but not boys) but has no detectable effect on BMI or the probability of obesity for either sex. A follow-up study (Cawley et al., 2013) estimates the impact of PE for younger children: those in elementary school. IV models that exploit variation across states in PE requirements and that are estimated using data from the Early Childhood Longitudinal Study, Kindergarten Class of 1998–1999 (ECLS-K), indicate that for children in kindergarten, 1st grade, or 3rd grade, PE has no detectable effect on weight. However, before the ECLS-K children reached 5th grade several populous states raised their PE requirements, and in the fifth grade wave the IV model indicates beneficial effects of PE; specifically, an additional $6 0 \mathrm { { m i n } }$ per week of PE reduces the probability of obesity by $4 . 8 \%$ points $( 2 2 \% )$ . This grade-specific result may be due to a difference in PE curriculum across grades, an age effect, the unusual number of state policy changes around that time, or No Child Left Behind leading to reductions in PE time for students in states without PE mandates. The result for 5th graders is concentrated among boys; parent-reported data on the youth participation in various activities suggest that PE is a complement with other physical activity for boys, but a substitute for other physical activity for girls. Overall, the results suggest that PE has no detectable effect on weight in most grades. However, it should be noted that this is the effect of the average PE curriculum; innovative PE programs that challenge and interest youth could be protective against obesity. Moreover, even if increased physical activity does not reduce weight, it has independent health benefits (IOM, 2012). 7.3. Genetic markers Genes are a particularly interesting natural experiment that epidemiologists refer to as Mendellian Randomization (Davey Smith and Ebrahim, 2005). Genes are an appealing source of variation because they are beyond the individual’s control and long precede the outcome – they are determined even before birth. However, to date it has proven challenging to use individual genes as instruments for obesity (Cawley et al., 2011). They tend not to be powerful instruments because, although genetic factors play an important role in obesity (Farooqi and O’Rahilly, 2007; Pietilainen, 2014) individual genes tend to have little independent influence on weight and geneticists’ understanding of those processes are far from complete; all known genetic polymorphisms combined explain less than $2 \%$ of the variance in obesity (Winter et al., 2013). There have also been challenges to validity; some studies have used as instruments alleles that, in addition to being only very weakly correlated with obesity, are associated with other risky behaviors and thus are likely to affect the outcome through channels other than obesity (see the discussion in Cawley et al., 2011). One of the strongest papers in this area is Von Hinke Kessler Scholder et al. (2012), which instruments for fat mass using the genetic marker FTO, which is highly correlated with fatness and does not seem to have the problems with validity that plagued genetic instruments used in earlier studies. As genetic research on obesity progresses, the suitability of specific genes as instruments in specific circumstances should become clearer. 8. Conclusion The large literature on the economics of obesity indicates that numerous economic variables, such as food prices, the time cost of food acquisition, income, education, the macroeconomy, and peer behaviors, may have modest effects on weight and obesity. The magnitude, and sometimes the sign, of these effects vary by subgroup (e.g. gender, race, age, and income). There appears to be no single dominant economic cause of obesity; instead, a wide variety of factors may each contribute a small amount, and different economic variables may be relevant for different groups. In contrast, the consequences of obesity are relatively clear: lower wages and higher medical care costs that impose negative externalities through health insurance. There exists an economic rationale for government intervention in order to internalize the negative externalities of obesity and provide information to consumers. Justifying government intervention on the grounds that consumers behave irrationally is contentious, and more widely accepted for children than adults. Research on economic approaches to treatment and prevention suggests that providing additional information through menu labels, taxing energy-dense foods, and offering financial rewards for weight loss, while justifiable as methods of addressing market failure, may have only modest effects on weight. Thus, just as there is no single cause of obesity there is no magic bullet that will reduce obesity; instead, a wide range of policies may be needed to have a substantial effect on the prevalence of obesity. An important caveat is that considerable research remains to be done to determine ways of making information, taxes, and financial rewards more effective in changing behavior. The large number of important research questions that remain suggests that the economics of obesity will continue to be an active and fruitful research area for many years to come.

I present new stylized facts on the market for managers over the twentieth century, utilizing a novel data set on managerial careers. From the 1930s to the mid-1970s, the level of executive pay, inequality among executives across and within firms, and mobility were low. These patterns have reversed since then. I document that an increase in the importance of general managerial human capital can account for this change. The level of general skills, measured by the type of education and occupational mobility of managers, correlate with higher pay and turnover. Other factors may have also contributed to these changes, but the labor market for managers has likely played an important role. Keywords: finance: corporate finance $\cdot$ management $\cdot$ organizational studies: personnel 1. Introduction The rapid rise in executive pay in the United States since the 1970s, particularly relative to the wages earned by other workers, has stimulated an extensive literature on executive compensation (Hall and Liebman 1998, Murphy 1999, Hall and Murphy 2003, Bebchuk and Fried 2003). Over this period, CEOs have also become increasingly mobile across firms (Huson et al. 2001). Surprisingly, the mobility and remuneration of top managers are often studied independently and, even when they are related, the workings of the labor market for executives receive little attention.1 This paper contributes new facts on the mobility, compensation, and careers of top executives over most of the twentieth century, with the aim of integrating the labor market to our understanding of the changes in pay and turnover. This long-run perspective suggests that an evolving market for corporate executives may have played an important role in the development of the compensation and mobility of top managers. An understanding of the long-run trends in the market for corporate executives has been hampered by a lack of consistent data (see Bertrand 2009 for a critical review of the literature). Using hand-collected information on the compensation and the biographies of about 1,000 executives from 1936 to 2003, I find that the level of total compensation and managerial turnover have followed a J-shaped pattern over this period. The inequality among top executives, both across and within firms, was relatively stable until the 1970s, but it has increased rapidly since then. The educational background and the experience of top managers have also evolved over time. I find that executives were more likely to obtain degrees in a technical discipline prior to the 1960s, but that formal education in business has become more common since then. Moreover, managers used to concentrate their expertise in one area (for example, rising to top leadership through various promotions in the sales sector exclusively) early in the twentieth century, but the diversity in their occupational experience has increased steadily over time. The changes in educational background and in occupational diversity are suggestive of a transformation in the types of managerial skills. I argue that the market for executives has increasingly placed more weight on general human capital, and less on firm-specific managerial skills. This shift may help to account for the changes in compensation and managerial mobility over the long run. To illustrate that such a shift in the type of skills could lead to an increase in pay, inequality, and mobility, I present an equilibrium model of the labor market for executives based on Murphy and Zábojnik (2004), Murphy and Zábojnik (2007). As in their framework, managerial ability is comprised of firm-specific and general skills, but only the latter are transferable across firms. I depart from their setup by studying the compensation of not only CEOs but also of other top executives in a model with search frictions. These frictions impede perfect assortative matching between executives and firms and introduce a wedge between a manager's compensation and her productivity within the firm. Specifically, managerial pay depends on the manager's outside option, which is determined by the executive's productivity in new firms. This outside option increases with the generality of managerial skills. In this framework, an increase in the importance of general skills leads to higher levels of compensation, higher turnover, and higher pay inequality. As general skills become more important, the manager's outside option increases, leading to higher equilibrium levels of executive pay. Turnover also rises for two reasons. First, higher levels of pay render low productivity firms unprofitable, which choose to stop operations. Second, high productivity firms endowed with low-ability managers choose to fire them because the benefit of hiring new managers on the job market is higher when those managers have higher levels of general skills. Finally, in the model the degree of skill generality determines the sensitivity of executive pay to managerial ability, but it also affects the endogenous allocation of talent across firms. In my setup, the first effect dominates; the distribution of executive pay both across all managers and among top managers within firms therefore widens with the increasing importance of general skills. To assess the model's predictions, I use principal components to create an index of the generality of human capital based on the education and occupational experience of managers, and relate it to pay and mobility. The predictions of the theoretical framework are borne out in the data. A one-standard deviation in the index is associated with an $1 1 \%$ increase in the annual level of pay, a $7 \%$ increase in managerial mobility (measured by the number of firms an executive worked for during his career), and an $8 \%$ increase in income inequality across top executives within the firm relative to the mean. Two important caveats should be taken into account when interpreting these magnitudes. First, the skill set of executives is obviously endogenous, and these estimates are therefore correlations. Understanding the determinants of the shift in observed managerial skills is important. Although a detailed analysis of the driving forces of such a shift exceeds the scope of the paper, several factors may have increased the demand for general managerial skills over the century. I discuss possible sources for this shift in Section 5. Second, the change in the types of managerial skills has been small relative to the large increases in the level of pay, inequality, and mobility. From the late 1930s to the early 2000s, managerial turnover increased by about $3 8 \% ,$ within-firm inequality among top managers rose by $6 5 \%$ , and the average level of total compensation in the sample increased by a staggering $8 7 0 \%$ . Thus, while the implied elasticities of pay, turnover, and inequality with respect to skill generality obtained from the regression analysis are substantial, it is likely that other factors also contributed to the sharp changes in these trends over time. This paper contributes to the large literature studying the determinants of executive compensation.² The importance of general managerial skills for the growth in CEO pay in recent years has been discussed both theoretically (Murphy and Zábojnik 2004, Murphy and Zábojnik 2007) and empirically (Custodio et al. 2013). I add to this literature by showing that a shift in the types of managerial skills may have contributed to the trends in compensation and in mobility over most of the twentieth century. Whether other countries have experienced a similar transformation is an interesting open question. Unfortunately, the United States is the only country to have required the disclosure of executive compensation in a systematic way for a long time period; instead, international comparisons are generally based on recent data (see, for example, Fernandes et al. 2013). Thus, this paper provides a unique longrun perspective on the market for corporate executives. A growing literature finds that CEO characteristics affect a variety of firm policies and outcomes (see, for example, Bertrand and Schoar 2003, Malmandier et al. 2011, Schoar and Zuo 2016). The novel long-run trends in managerial careers that I put forth show that CEO characteristics have evolved greatly over time. An open question for future research is to study whether these new stylized facts have had consequences for firm outcomes over the twentieth century. Executive compensation, turnover, and career paths are complex phenomena, and it is therefore unlikely that a single factor could account for the evolution of these measures over 70 years. In Section $5 ~ \mathrm { I }$ discuss other factors that have probably contributed to the long-run trends. However, the findings of this paper suggest that the labor market has played an important, but relatively ignored, role in this process. 4.2. \begin{tcolorbox}[title={Stage 1 System Prompt}, breakable]
\begin{verbatim}
# Role
You are an expert AI Research Assistant specializing in causal claim from economics literature. Your goal is to extract high-fidelity causal claims to construct a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG).

# Goal
Extract substantive causal relationships while filtering out logical fallacies, definitional tautologies, and background literature review. 

# Global Rules
1. **NO Tautology & Definitions**: If A is a component of B, a mathematical indicator of B, or a definition of B, EXCLUDE it. (e.g., "Diversification Index -> Covariance" is a calculation, not causation).
2. **NO Self-Causation**: Reject claims where A and B are semantically identical (e.g., "Overconfidence -> Overconfidence in detection").
3. **NO Literature Theft**: Extract ONLY the original findings/contributions of the current paper. Exclude background context, cited previous studies (e.g., "Foley (1967) shows..."), or common knowledge.
4. **Entity Resolution**: Merge synonymous concepts. If the paper uses "Extensive margin" and "Probability of entry" interchangeably, map them to a single consistent node name.
6. **Theory vs. Empirics**: 
   - For Empirical papers: Extract `Variable A -> [Sign] -> Variable B`.
   - For Theoretical papers: Extract `Assumption/Constraint -> [Prevents/Guarantees] -> Equilibrium Outcome`. 
   - Reject vague system states like "Compatibility" or "Existence" as outcome nodes unless they are specific, measurable variables.
7. You MUST output valid JSON only.

# Field Dictionary & Extraction Instructions

**1. edges (Array of objects)**:
Do not repeat the same claim.

For each claim, you MUST specify:

- **claim (String)**: 'A -> B' format. 
  - **Constraint**: Nodes A and B MUST be pure, neutral noun phrases. 
  - **Action**: Use the "Sign_of_impact" field to describe the movement, not the node name (e.g., use "Interest Rate", not "Higher Interest Rate").

- **cause (String)**: The causal variable. Must be a specific economic entity.

- **effect (String)**: The outcome variable. Must be a concrete, measurable, or theoretically defined entity.

- **sign_of_impact (Enum)**: [CRITICAL] Select EXACTLY ONE:
  - `positive`: A increases B.
  - `negative`: A decreases B.
  - `null_effect`: A has no statistically significant impact on B (The paper explicitly finds a zero effect).
  - `u_shaped`: Non-linear relationship.
  - `ambiguous`: Relationship depends on other moderators.

- **type_of_relationship**:  Select EXACTLY ONE from:["direct effect", "indirect effect", "confounding", "mediation", "collider", "ancestor", "descendant", "bidirectional", "association", "other"]


- **evidence (String)**: **[CRITICAL]** Provide the comprehensive verbatim text block that explicitly proves EVERY attribute below. A single summary sentence is NEVER enough.Search across the ENTIRE text and concatenate relevant sentences using "[...]".If the text contains pronouns (e.g., "it", "they", "this effect"), keep the original sentence unchanged and add a clarification in parentheses at the end of the sentence indicating what the pronoun refers to.**EVERY non-NA value you populate in the subsequent fields MUST have its exact verbatim proof physically present in this evidence string. If verbatim proof for a specific attribute does not exist, you MUST output 'NA' for that attribute.

- **causal_inference_method(Enum)**:  Explicitly list all methods used, strictly distinguishing causal identification from correlational/theoretical analyses. If mixed methods are used, list each separately.Select EXACTLY from: ["RDD", "DID", "RCT", "IV", "Structural Estimation", "Fixed Effects Models", "Event Study", "Simulation", "Matching Methods", "Synthetic Controls", "VAR", "Theoretical/Non-Empirical", "Machine Learning Methods", "Bayesian Methods", "Other", "Do not know"]

- **evidence_method_other_description (String)**: If causal_inference_method = "Other", describe the method using verbatim text.Otherwise, output "NA".


- **sources_of_exogenous_variation(String)**:  Identify sources of exogenous variation used for identification (e.g., 'Variation in the timing of reliability projects', 'Infertility shocks', 'Regional variation in heat stress'). If not mentioned, write 'NA'.
-  level_of_tentativeness(Enum): The level of tentativeness or certainty in the author's evidence. Must be exactly one of: ['certain', 'tentative'].

- **statistical_significance (Enum)**: ['p<0.01', '0.01<=p<0.05', '0.05<=p<0.1', 'p>0.1', 'NA']

- **is_main_contribution (Boolean)**: Set to `true` ONLY if this is a primary finding of the paper. Set to `false` if it's a robust check or secondary result.

# Output Format
You MUST output valid JSON only.
Do not include markdown, explanation, or extra text.

\end{verbatim}

Here is a text extract from an economics paper: Maternal education and child mortality in Zimbabwe Karen A. Grépina,∗, Prashant Bharadwaj b a Robert F. Wagner Graduate School of Public Service, New York University, 295 Lafayette Street, 3rd Floor, New York, NY 10012, USA b Department of Economics, University of California, San Diego, 9500 Gilman Drive No. 0508, La Jolla, San Diego, CA 92093, USA a r t i c l e i n f o Abstract Article history: Received 10 December 2014 Received in revised form 5 August 2015 Accepted 7 August 2015 Available online 24 August 2015 JEL classification: I15 I12 I26 J13 O12 N37 Keywords: Maternal education Returns to education Child mortality Fertility Natural experiment In 1980, Zimbabwe rapidly expanded access to secondary schools, providing a natural experiment to estimate the impact of increased maternal secondary education on child mortality. Exploiting age specific exposure to these reforms, we find that children born to mothers most likely to have benefited from the policies were about $2 1 \%$ less likely to die than children born to slightly older mothers. We also find that increased education leads to delayed age at marriage, sexual debut, and first birth and that increased education leads to better economic opportunities for women. We find little evidence supporting other channels through which increased education might affect child mortality. Expanding access to secondary schools may greatly accelerate declines in child mortality in the developing world today. $^ { © }$ 2015 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved. 1. Introduction Across the world, studies have generally found that more educated people live longer and healthier lives, and they give birth to fewer but healthier children (Grossman, 2006). However, only a few of these studies have been able to identify causal evidence of the impact of education, and very few studies have been conducted in the developing world (Lochner, 2011). In addition, very few studies have been able to investigate mechanisms through which improved education might affect health outcomes. Given the disproportionate share of the burden of disease as well as persistently high child mortality and fertility rates in developing countries, there is a need to better understand what role education might play in improving development outcomes today. The major challenge to better understanding these relationships has been identifying situations in which education has increased in a way that is unrelated to other factors that might also affect health. The most successful studies have looked at natural experiments, usually changes in compulsory schooling laws or age-at-entry policies, to identify plausibly exogenous changes in education. Generally, most of these studies have found that increased levels of education are associated with lower (own) mortality, improved healthy behaviors (including smoking), lower fertility, and lower child mortality; however, not all of the studies come to the same conclusions1. Although evidence is sparse, there is also some evidence that educating mothers might lead to different outcomes than educating fathers, and that higher levels of schooling may be more important than primary schooling (Lochner, 2011). In 1980, following independence, Zimbabwe rapidly expanded access to secondary schools for black Zimbabweans, which provides an opportunity to estimate the impact of increased maternal secondary education on child health and fertility outcomes in a setting with both high child mortality and high fertility2. Using age-specific exposure to a set of policies that greatly increased secondary school opportunities for some women, we first estimate the impact of increased maternal education on child survival3. The magnitude of our main result is large: children born to mothers who attended some secondary schooling are 12 percentage points less likely to die, and an additional year of schooling decreases the probability of a child dying by about $2 1 \%$ . We find that the effects are much stronger in rural areas and among less wealthy mothers. We next examine important pathways that might explain the relationship between maternal education and child survival. Since the data from the DHS are quite detailed, we examine mechanisms that encompass the broad categories of fertility (age at marriage, first birth, etc.), economic outcomes (household asset ownership, spousal quality, etc.), health service utilization (institutional delivery and vaccinations) and female empowerment (control over household finances and attitudes toward domestic violence). These outcomes are related to the classic theories of how education may improve health directly via allocative efficiency or productive efficiency mechanisms (Grossman, 2006) or indirectly through some of the other benefits of education such as increased income. For example, a mother’s education may directly affect a child’s health outcomes if it influences the likelihood that she completes all required pre-natal visits, she fully vaccinates her children, or she makes more informed choices with regards to healthcare providers. Alternatively, a more educated mother may have more economic opportunities and she may use these to gain access to more or better quality health care providers. As in McCrary and Royer (2011), we cannot distinguish between direct and indirect channels via which maternal education might affect child health. The health services provided to children of women were examined since it is believed that mothers have a great deal of discretion over the services that their children receive and because timely and more adherent treatment has been linked to improved child health outcomes. Across these broad categories, we find evidence that education affects fertility and economic opportunity related outcomes, but we find little evidence on other channels. It is crucial to highlight that while Zimbabwean independence brought about other changes beyond expanding secondary schooling (Thomas and Maluccio, 1996), we exploit the idea that being 13 years of age and younger in 1980 allowed one to have greater access to secondary school as opposed to being a few years older and therefore less likely to take advantage of the opportunity to attend secondary school; the operating assumption in this paper is that the other broader changes due to independence did not differentially affect those just below and those just above 13 in 1980. We assess the validity of this assumption by examining mortality outcomes of children born to mothers who had dropped out of school by age 9. These are mothers who did not take advantage of the educational reforms. Hence, if simply being of a certain age during independence is a driving factor for our results, we should find that children of those mothers below 13 in 1980 and those children born to slightly older mothers to have very different mortality outcomes even in this sample, however, we do not find any effect in this sample. In addition, we also include year of birth fixed-effects for the children born to these women, in order to account for any year-specific trends that could have affected all children. Finally, we also examine the trends in child mortality in Zimbabwe before and after independence and find that child mortality rates were relatively stable during the time period when the most of the births in our sample take place. Furthermore, we examine a few outcomes that are determined before independence, and outcomes that are not affected by education, and we find that just being of a certain age during independence is not driving our results. It should also be stressed that we examine the outcomes of children born many years after independence. Hence, if independence was accompanied by a better health system, then all children born after 1980 (regardless of when their mothers turned 13) would be exposed to the same postindependence health system. We find that even among children born many years after independence, those whose mothers happened to be below 13 in 1980 have better survival outcomes than those whose mothers were just too old to have benefited from the policy changes in the education sector. This paper is part of a number of studies that have looked specifically at the role of maternal education in improving health and fertility outcomes. Among developed countries, the opening of colleges to women in the United States has been linked to higher infant birth weight, increased gestational age at birth and lower fertility (Currie and Moretti, 2003; Grossman, 2006). Increases in compulsory years of education in Norway has also been linked to relatively large increases in weight at birth to children born to exposed women (Grytten et al., 2014; Lochner, 2011). However, children of women born in months just before primary school month-of-entry policies (who, hence, receive more education than women born in months just after such cut offs) in some parts of the United States were no healthier than babies born to women just after these cut offs, suggesting that not all gains in education have the same effect (Lochner, 2011; McCrary and Royer, 2011). In the developing world, a handful of studies have investigated the role of expanded access to primary schooling on child health and fertility outcomes. A policy that led to increased years of compulsory primary education in Turkey has been linked to lower fertility and increased use of contraception (Dinc¸ er et al., 2014) as well as less low birth weight babies and healthier children (Gunes, 2013). The introduction of universal primary education in Nigeria has been linked to lower early fertility among exposed women (Osili and Long, 2008). In a working paper, (Breierova and Duflo, 2004) use a large primary school construction program in Indonesia in the 1970s to find that female education was linked to delayed marriage and lower fertility, while the education of both parents was associated with lower child mortality. While our paper is similar in spirit, Breierova and Duflo (2004) have a rather weak first stage and are unable to examine detailed mechanisms. A few studies have also investigated the impact of higher levels of education on health outcomes in the developing world. In Taiwan, an increase in the number of years of compulsory schooling (from 6 to 9 years), affecting mostly junior high school aged children, coupled with a large school construction program has been linked to improved infant health outcomes, including a reduction in low birth weight children and a small decrease in infant mortality (Chou et al., 2010). A similar expansion of compulsory schooling from 6th to 9th grade in Mexico has been linked to increased use of contraception (Andalón et al., 2014). Evidence from the long-term follow-up of a large-scale randomized experiment which reduced the costs of education for adolescent girls in Kenya found that increased retention of students in schools was associated with lower teenage pregnancy rates (Duflo et al., 2014). Similarly, teenage girls in Malawi who were induced to stay in school through a cash transfer program also had lower teenage pregnancy rates (Baird et al., 2011). A study that investigated the impact of a large high school closure program in China, which uniquely employed an identification strategy from a policy change that led to lower levels of maternal education, found no impact of maternal education on child health outcomes (Zhang, 2012). It is notable that fertility rates in China at the time of this policy change were already very low by international standards. While all but two of the studies mentioned above support the view that increased education leads to improvements in child health, improved healthy behaviors, and lower fertility, none have looked specifically at the role of maternal secondary education that result from a national policy change in s setting with very high rates of child mortality and high rates of fertility (in Taiwan and China, rates of child mortality and fertility in the 1960s were already low by standards of most developing countries today). Rates of fertility and child mortality have remained persistently high in much of Sub-Saharan Africa, the same region where there have been the fewest gains in secondary schooling globally (Mingat et al., 2010). Given the importance of reducing child mortality globally, a better understanding of the role of maternal secondary education in improving child health and fertility in specifically these types of settings is thus important from a policy perspective. 4.1. First stage results: Impact of policy changes on maternal education Fig. 1 demonstrates the effects of the reforms on the educational attainment of all women in the DHS (not just those in our samples) with age of the women in 1980 presented along the $x$ -axis. There are two vertical lines in each figure at age 14 and 15, the ages that we consider partially treated. The women immediately on the left hand side of the vertical bars are considered the treatment group, and the women immediately on the right side are the control group (again we show data on all women in the DHS, not just those in our samples). The discontinuity is easily visible: women who were less than 13 in 1980 experienced a greater jump in schooling relative to those who were 16 or older in 1980. Table 2 summarizes the results of our first stage regressions: the discontinuity in education is associated with an increase in education of 1.68 years and an increased probability of attending some secondary school by 25.2 percentage points, after controlling for other variables. It is worth noting that these are very large and very rapid increases in both the number of year and probability of attending any secondary schooling. Table 2 also shows that the first stage is stronger in rural areas and among people with a low wealth index. In Appendix Fig. A1, we show that all provinces in Zimbabwe experienced increases in educational achievement and that this indeed was a country-wide expansion of schooling. We also include estimates of the impact of the educational policy on women who were 14 and 15 in 1980, and the effects are somewhat diminished, which makes sense since these women were only partially treated. In Table 2, we also demonstrate that our first stage results are also robust to the inclusion of polynomials in age in 1980 and with larger bandwidths in our sample. 4.2. Impact on child survival Fig. 2a charts the mortality of children born to all women in our sample. We see a discontinuous decrease in the probability of child death, which appears to coincide with the timing of the increases in maternal education. Note that the figures only tell us the difference in survival by the age of the mother in 1980, whereas the regressions, due to the instrumental variable approach, tell us the increase in survival due to an extra year of education, the results of which are presented in Table 3. One extra year of maternal education was associated with a 1.7 percentage point decrease in the probability that a child was reported to have died prior to the survey. Given that on average $7 . 9 \%$ of the children in our sample were reported to have died at the time of the survey, the decrease in child mortality from one year of education represents an approximately $2 1 . 5 \%$ decrease in child deaths. Table 3 also shows that OLS estimates of this relationship tend to be severely underestimated. Additionally, Table 3 reveals that the effects on mortality by a certain age (5 years or 1 year) are largely similar, negative and statistically significant. Child deaths are heavily concentrated in the early years of life, which is consistent with known patterns of child mortality. This is important, since our primary measure of child survival includes all children ever born to the women in the DHS surveys, including children who may be teenagers or adults by the later surveys. We also test an alternative outcome – mortality by age 5 and mortality by age 1 – to rule out, for example, the rise of HIV among youth.
