Desired fertility, on the other hand, does seem to be strongly affected by schooling. Women with more schooling desire fewer children and, as Table 6 suggests, 0.22 children less off a base of 4.5 children. This result is robust to polynomial trends on either side of the discontinuity, and importantly, as can be seen from Fig. 3, there appears to be a real trend break around the discontinuity in the number of children desired. We then examine outcomes such as female empowerment (see Section 2 and Appendix A on how this variable is created), opinions on domestic violence and risky behavior (smoking) in Table 7, and we find very little evidence that schooling plays an important role in affecting these outcomes. In the lower half of Table 7, we examine economic outcomes of the mother and find that asset ownership, urban location, and probability of working are higher for the more educated. We also define two dummy variables: one for being in the lowest wealth quintile and another for being in the highest wealth quintile. We find that more education is associated with a lower probability of being in the lowest wealth quintile, which is likely related to the changes in the probability of having electricity and living in a rural area. Appendix Table A3 shows that the coefficients on urban location and probability of working are robust to polynomial trends in age; however, we wish to stress some caution in reading too much into these results as the reduced form results in Fig. 4 do not show clear trend breaks in these outcomes around the cutoff. Taken together, we interpret the results of Tables 6 and 7 to suggest that schooling appears to affect fertility decisions and some economic outcomes that might be relevant for child survival. Education does not seem to affect outcomes related to the woman’s status in the household, although we admit that these are relatively noisy measures in the DHS. It is important to also examine the impact of the reform on male schooling in order to determine if the results we observe are being driven by maternal education, paternal education or changes in marriage match quality that result after the school expansion. While it is rather difficult to completely disentangle these effects, we explore these possibilities in Fig. 5 and conclude that changes in maternal education are most likely driving our results. A few things are important to note in Fig. 5. First, the age specificity of the reform is less strict for men, both due to pre-independence higher rates of school attendance and perhaps also a higher likelihood of re-enrolling after independence. Second, there is no discontinuity in the age of men that women marry, and while the reform also affected men, the fact that age of husbands does not shift around the cutoff (note that women marry men who are on average 5 years older) suggests that husband’s education is likely not that different around the cutoff (bottom left in Fig. 5). Third, the bottom-right graph in Fig. 5 shows that, consistent with this idea, the most significant change among couples wherein the woman is below 14 or 15 in 1980 is the difference in educational attainment between husbands and wives. Women who experienced increased schooling have a smaller gap in educational attainment compared to women who were too old to take advantage of the reforms. These figures lend support to the notion that changes in maternal education around the time of the reform are the most important drivers of the educational reforms on child mortality. We also recognize that these results can be interpreted as suggesting that what might matter for outcomes is not maternal education per se but the difference in husband versus wife’s education. We cannot disentangle these effects in the current design.

The next set of outcomes we examine in Table 8 is related to the health-seeking behavior of the mother on behalf of her child. In Table 8, maternal education appears to have no statistically significant effect on institutional deliveries (which is surprising given the apparent jump visible in Fig. 6), but it has a large and statistically significant effect on delivery via cesarean section. The cesarean section rate in our sample is relatively low, but the magnitude of the result suggests that an extra year of education increases the likelihood of a cesarean section by nearly $8 5 \%$ . Interestingly, maternal education seems to have no effect on preventive health care acts such as antenatal care and full immunizations, although these rates are high in the full sample. These results are shown graphically in Fig. 6. Using household surveys to measure health service utilization has been shown to be prone to different forms of bias, however, with no clear generalizable patterns for the bias, in particular in low and middle income countries (Miles et al., 2013). While we might expect women of higher education to more accurately report health service use, the fact that we observe little significant effects of education on any of the health service utilization variables we investigate causes us to believe recall bias didn’t have a major effect in driving our findings on health service utilization. Where reporting biases has been analyzed in the context of diarrhea, investigators found very little differences in accuracy of reported rates between mothers with primary and secondary education, the most relevant margin for this study (Boerma et al., 1991). It is worth highlighting that we test health-seeking behaviors among the most recent births but child mortality in all births of the women in our sample. We therefore replicate our child mortality results in the sample of recent births in the bottom panel of Table 8. We find that the results are very similar in magnitude but and statistically significant at conventional levels despite diminished sample size (Table 8 uses only $2 0 \%$ of the data used in Table 3). 4.4. Robustness tests As stated earlier, an important concern is that independence led to other changes, beyond those in the education sector—although why this would occur differentially for those just below and above 13 is perhaps a harder argument to make. Our first attempt at capturing the possibility that other reforms or changes might differentially affect those below 13 in 1980 is to examine our main child mortality outcome for women who had dropped out by age 9 and, hence, never took advantage of the reforms (we repeated this exercise for dropouts by age 10 or 11 and the results looked very similar)5. Fig. 7 shows that there is no discontinuity in child mortality around age 14 or 15 for women who dropped out of school years before independence. Hence, it seems unlikely that independence led to other reforms that had age-specific effects that could explain our results. We also plot child mortality relative to the year of birth of the children in Fig. 8. We see that there were large declines in child mortality that began in the mid-1970s but that by 1983, child mortality rates had largely stabilized and remained relatively constant through the 2000s. There is no discontinuity in child mortality at independence itself, rather the continuation in a trend that began prior to independence. This pattern is consistent with a decline in mortality as the country transitioned out of civil war before independence and which researchers predicted in the 1980s, despite the lack of data to measure child mortality at the time. It is also consistent with evidence from the 1980s that suggested that most of the changes within the health care sector happened within the first few years after independence, but then stabilized or eventually faded out (Loewenson et al., 1991). Since the average age of first birth of the women in our sample was 19 years old, most of the births in our sample of children would have occurred after the major declines in child mortality in this figure occurred. Given that the women in our control group were slightly older than women in the treatment group it may be that more children of control group mothers were born during a time period with higher prevailing child mortality rates, which could account for some of the differences in child mortality we observe between groups. To help rule this out, we conduct two additional analyses, which are presented in Appendix Tables A4a and A4b. First, we update our main results on child mortality on samples that exclude all children born in or prior to the years 1980 through 1985. Given that the average year of birth in our sample is in the late 1980s, unsurprisingly we don’t lose a lot of sample by excluding these additional children and our estimates remain largely unchanged, suggesting our main findings are not being driven by births that occurred during the early 1980s. Second, we also do a similar exercise but instead exclude all women whose first births occurred in or prior to the years 1980 through 1985. This is a much stricter restriction on our sample and so we face a much greater challenge in maintaining sample size, but again we find that the results are relatively consistent to our main findings and robust to this additional test. Given that our findings suggest that the reduction in child mortality was driven primarily through a delay in the age of first birth, we further investigate the changes in fertility in our samples. At independence, contraceptive rates were relatively low in Zimbabwe, and the national family planning program had been deemed largely inefficient. Although family planning programs had existed in Zimbabwe since 1964, only about $1 4 \%$ of married women aged 15–49 were using any form of modern contraception at independence (Boohene and Dow, 1987). In 1981, the family planning programs were reorganized and integrated within the Ministry of Health and over the next few years underwent significant operational changes. They also adopted a new strategy that focused heavily on community-based distribution, information and education, as well as improvements in the supply of modern family planning programs (Boohene and Dow, 1987). By the mid-1980s, the contraceptive prevalence rate among married women had increased substantially; however, there was very little observed decline in fertility overall, suggesting that most of the increased use of contraceptives was likely being used by women to increase birth spacing (Boohene and Dow, 1987). In Table 7, we found a small effect of increased education on the use of modern contraception that was only significant at the $1 0 \%$ level. Furthermore, in Fig. 9, we chart the trends in birth spacing among the women in our sample. While there is a clear trend toward longer birth intervals among younger women, there is no discontinuity visible at the ages corresponding to the increase in education. Our findings strongly suggest that the biggest effect of increased maternal education on fertility appears to have been largely mechanical: an important shift in the age at cohabitation and of first birth. And, while education appears to have affected the desire to have fewer children, we find little effect on actual fertility, suggesting that access to contraception was unlikely to have been made available in an age-specific manner that could be undermining our results. While it is common for regression discontinuity design based papers to show “smoothness of covariates”, this is particularly difficult to do in our case since the DHS does not collect data on a rich set of variables that were likely to be determined prior to early adolescence. Hence, almost any outcome in the DHS could have been affected by increased education. In Fig. 10, we show that sex of the child, the religion of the mother, the number of women sampled and the year of survey are quite smooth around the point of discontinuity. Moreover, show that height of the mother (determined in early childhood) is also not affected around the discontinuity. A related concern is that of differential mortality of the mother: if the more educated are less (or more) likely to be surveyed or less (or more) likely to die, then such sample selection could bias our results. Even though Appendix Fig. A2 shows that the histogram of ages is smooth around the cutoff, we further explore this possibility in a few different ways. First, using the module on maternal mortality in the DHS, we examine the likelihood of the female siblings of the respondent dying due to pregnancy-related reasons by age of the sister in 1980 and conditional on the sister being alive in 1980. Appendix Fig. A3 suggests that differential pregnancy-related mortality due to increased education is likely not an issue. Using data on all siblings (male or female) of the respondent in Appendix Fig. A4, we assess the probability that any individual sibling is alive in 1980 and whether any individual sibling is likely to be dead after 1980 conditional on being alive in 1980 (in other words, the top right graph of Appendix Fig. A4 shows that there does not appear to be a discontinuity in adult mortality as a result of increased education). In the bottom panel of Appendix Fig. A4, we examine whether sibling structure is differential around the cutoff and find that it is not. These figures help add evidence suggesting that what was mainly different for those just below and just above the age of 13 in 1980 was access to schooling. Finally, evidence presented in using data from neighboring countries shows that not all countries experienced an increase in educational enrollment starting in the 1980s (see Fig. 5. 5. Discussion and conclusions A number of channels have been postulated as ways in which education might lead to changes in child mortality and other health outcomes. First, education may make people more efficient producers of health (the productive efficiency hypothesis), which could make people more adherent to treatments or make people get more health out of the same inputs. Second, education may make people more aware of different treatments, which may lead them to make different choices with regards to preventive behaviors or different treatments (the allocative efficiency hypothesis). Third, increased education might lead to higher incomes, which could directly affect health by increasing the purchasing power of individuals (income effects). Finally, there are also a number of additional pathways, which might influence one or more of these channels in less wellestablished ways, such as the propensity to marry a better partner, social networks, etc. Our study provides causal evidence of the impact of maternal education on child mortality and explores some potential channels underlying this effect. We find a robust effect on child survival and find supporting evidence toward channels that involve fertility and economic outcomes due to increased education. We do not find support for mechanisms that involve health-seeking behavior or female empowerment. It is notable that these effects seem to have occurred in a setting where the quality of secondary education is reportedly quite poor. Our findings suggest that education may have largely had an incapacitation effect, in the sense that it mechanically delayed age at cohabitation and fertility. Had the quality of education been improved, there might have been additional effects, and it might also help to explain little changes in health-seeking behavior or other outcomes. We note that the educational reforms in Zimbabwe differed from many of the previous natural experiments investigated that were compulsory in nature, since enrolling into secondary school was still voluntary post-Independence. Compulsory schooling and voluntary expansions to schooling will capture different local average treatment effect (LATE). In a world of compulsory schooling, it is possible that those children whose returns to schooling are the lowest are now the marginal children who are pushed (by law) into attending school. In our case, the children on the margin might be children whose returns to schooling might be high, but costs also sufficiently high, that prior to the reforms, these children did not go to school. Hence, when costs are lowered and schooling is not compulsory, those with the highest returns might select into schooling, while those with low returns, despite the lower costs, choose to stay out of school. Hence, compulsory schooling and expanded access to schooling measures capture two rather different LATEs depending on the assumptions we make about how each of the reforms change the returns to and costs of schooling. Those familiar with Zimbabwe are undoubtedly aware of other changes that have happened in this country over the past few decades, including the rapid spread of HIV and the near collapse of the public health system (Todd et al., 2010). However, we believe our empirical approach can rule out most of these changes as potential alternative explanations due to the age-specific structure of our analysis. While another study suggested that Zimbabwean women who benefited from the same policy change were more likely to be aware of HIV and its modes of transmission, there is no evidence that these women were more or less likely to acquire HIV/AIDS. At the time of independence, Zimbabwe was a well-off country relative to other countries in Sub-Saharan Africa; it had relatively high levels of literacy and high levels of primary education, but secondary education rates were still low. Moreover, under-5 mortality in Zimbabwe in 1980 was approximately 100 per 1000 live births, and the total fertility rate was just over 7, which would make it comparable to the rates in many African countries today. Like improving health, increasing education is also an important development priority. Millennium Development Goal (MDG) 2, a goal to achieve universal primary education, has been among the most successful MDGs: primary education enrollment in developing regions reached nearly $9 0 \%$ by 2011 (Go and Quijada, 2012). Primary education rates for girls have improved the most and are now nearly on par with those of boys, even in the poorest regions in the world. However, there has been substantially less progress with regards to secondary education, in particular in the least developed countries of Sub-Saharan Africa, where child mortality rates remain high (Mingat et al., 2010). Our findings suggest that increasing maternal secondary education might be an effective way to reduce child mortality and fertility rates in the developing world today.

Dually-Weighted Cross Decomposition for the Capacitated Facility Location Problem
Paul Wentges Institut für Unternehmensforschung der Hochschule St. Gallen Bodanstr. 6, 9000 St. Gallen, Switzerland 
Abstract
The cross decomposition algorithm of [van Roy 1986] is generally considered to be one of the most efficient procedures for solving the capacitated facility location problem. A modified version of this algorithm, called dually-weighted cross decomposition, is presented. In contrast to the cross decomposition algorithm, this approach does not use the optimal dual solutions of the primal subproblems or the optimal solutions of the dual master problem as Lagrangean multipliers for the dual subproblems. A specially weighted average of the previously constructed multipliers is used instead. Finite convergence of this approach is proven and first promising results are discussed. 
1 Introduction
The capacitated facility location problem (CFLP) can be formulated as the following mixedinteger programming problem (see e.g. [Cornuejols et al. 1991] for a more detailed description of the problem) : 
$$
 C F L P \middle > \{ \begin{array} { l l } { \displaystyle \operatorname* { m i n } \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } f _ { j } y _ { j } + \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } c _ { i j } x _ { i j } , } \\ { \displaystyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } x _ { i j } = d _ { i } \forall i , } \\ { \displaystyle x _ { i j } \leq d _ { i } y _ { j } \ \forall i , j , } \\ { \displaystyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } x _ { i j } \leq s _ { j } y _ { j } \ \forall j , } \\ { \displaystyle \operatorname* { m i n } _ { x _ { i j } \geq 0 , \ y _ { j } \in \ \{ 0 , 1 \} \ \forall i , j , } } \end{array} 
$$
where $_ m$ represents the number of customers, $n$ the number of potential facility locations, $d _ { i }$ the demand of customer $_ i$ , and $s _ { j }$ the capacity of facility $j$ . $c _ { i j }$ are the costs to transport one unit from facility $j$ to customer $_ i$ and $f _ { j }$ the fixed costs to maintain/build facility $j$ . The variable $y _ { j }$ indicates whether facility $j$ is opened $( y _ { j } = 1 )$ or not, and $\boldsymbol { x } _ { i j }$ represents the amount shipped from facility $j$ to customer $_ i$ . 
The cross decomposition algorithm of [van Roy 1986] simultaneously exploits both the primal structure (temporarily fixing the variables $_ y$ yields a normal transportation problem) and the dual structure (with relaxing the capacity constraints (3) in lagrangean fashion) of the (CFLP), i. e. combines Benders' decomposition and Dantzig-Wolfe decomposition in one single framework. The approach is motivated by the fact, that the primal subproblem can be viewed as a relaxed dual (Dantzig-Wolfe) master problem and the dual subproblem as a relaxed primal (Benders) master problem (see e.g. [van Roy 1983]). 
The main steps of the algorithm can be described as follows (let $( S D _ { \mu } )$ be the Lagrangean relaxation of $( C F L P )$ with respect to the capacity constraints (3) and the Lagrangean multipliers $\mu$ b $( M D _ { k } )$ the relaxed Dantzig-Wolfe master problem: $\textstyle \operatorname* { m a x } \{ \delta : \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } f _ { j } y _ { j } ^ { t } +$ $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } c _ { i j } x _ { i j } ^ { t } - \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } ( s _ { j } y _ { j } ^ { t } - \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } x _ { i j } ^ { t } ) \mu _ { j } \geq \delta \forall t \in T _ { k } ; } \end{array}$ $\mu \geq 0 , \delta \in \mathbb { R } \}$ $( S P _ { y } )$ the transportation problem obtained when $_ y$ is fixed, and $( M P _ { k } )$ a relaxed Benders master problem; for a more detailed and explicit description of the problems see [van Roy 1986]): 
Step 1: Initialize and get a dual solution $\mu ^ { 1 }$ (by solving the primal subproblem $( S P _ { y ^ { 0 } } )$ with $y ^ { 0 } \equiv 1$ ).   
Step 2: Solve the dual subproblem $( S D _ { \mu ^ { k } } )$ : Let $( x ^ { k } , y ^ { k } )$ be an optimal solution. Perform a convergence test; if the test is not fulfilled, go to step 5.   
Step 3: Solve the primal subproblem $( S P _ { y ^ { k } } )$ : Let $( \lambda ^ { k + 1 } , \nu ^ { k + 1 } , \mu ^ { k + 1 } )$ be an optimal dual solution. Perform a convergence test; if the test is not fulfilled, go to step 5 (or step 4, see below), otherwise go to step 2 and set $k : = k + 1$ .   
Step 4: Solve the primal master problem $\left( M P _ { k } \right)$ : Let $y ^ { k + 1 }$ be an optimal solution. Go to step 3 and set $k : = k + 1$ .   
Step 5: Solve the dual master problem $( M D _ { k } )$ : Let $\mu ^ { k + 1 }$ be an optimal solution. Go to step 2 and set $k : = k + 1$ . 
In steps 2 and 3, cuts corresponding to the optimal solutions have to be added to the respective master problems; in each step, optimality has to be checked. If the Lagrangean dual is solved within a specified tolerance level $\tau$ (e.g. $0 . 5 \%$ ), one switches to Benders' decomposition (only usage of steps 3 and 4). 
The cross decomposition algorithm solves the (CFLP) in a finite number of steps, since the convergence tests prevent the algorithm from cycling and therefore, after finitely many steps, the method amounts to Benders' decomposition, which is known to be finite (see e.g. [van Roy 1983] and [Holmberg 1990], respectively).

Using the Canadian National Population Health Survey from 1994 to 2003 and implementing a difference-in-differences estimation strategy, we find that the mandatory program substantially increased drug coverage among the general population. The program also increased medication use and general practitioner visits but had little effect on specialist visits and hospitalization. Findings from quantile regressions suggest that there was a large improvement in the health status of less healthy individuals. Further analysis by pre-policy drug insurance status and the presence of chronic conditions reveals a marked increase in the probability of taking medication and visiting a general practitioner among the previously uninsured and those with a chronic condition. $^ { © }$ 2015 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved. 1. Introduction Pharmaceutical drug expenditure accounts for a significant proportion of overall health spending in many OECD countries. On average, more than a sixth of total health expenditure was dedicated to pharmaceuticals across OECD countries in 2011. On a per capita basis, the United States spend the most, almost USD 1000, followed by Canada (OECD, 2013). The rising financial burden associated with prescription drugs has raised policy concerns about the optimal design of health insurance, and drug insurance in particular, to ensure access to affordable prescription drugs. For example, the Part D drug benefit was added to Medicare in the United States (The Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act of 2003). Several OECD countries, such as New Zealand, United Kingdom, the Netherlands and Germany, provide universal coverage for prescription drugs, which is integrated into the broader system of public health insurance or statutory social health insurance policies (Morgan et al., 2013). Unlike physician and hospital services, which are universal in Canada, coverage for prescription drugs dispensed outside hospitals falls outside the Canada Health Act and provincial governments only provide public drug programs for some population groups, primarily seniors and social assistance recipients. A number of provincial and territorial governments introduced some form of catastrophic drug coverage with high deductibles for certain groups in the past decade (Daw and Morgan, 2012; Daw et al., 2013) but there has been little progress on a national pharmacare program. Most non-elderly Canadians who have drug insurance obtain it through employee benefit plans. However, a significant number of Canadians are un-insured or under-insured against the costs of prescription drugs (Kapur and Basu, 2005). About one in 10 Canadians who receive a prescription report cost-related non-adherence, and the lack of drug insurance coverage appears to be a key reason behind this phenomenon (Law et al., 2012). How to reform Canada’s pharmaceutical drug coverage has been under active discussion in Canada since the late 1990s. A number of recommendations for a national pharmacare program have been proposed, such as expanding universal public system to include first-dollar of prescription drugs (National Forum on Health, 1997) or protecting Canadians against catastrophic drug expenses through a catastrophic drug plan (Romanow Commission on the Future of Health Care in Canada, 2002; Standing Senate Committee on Social Affairs, Science and Technology, 2002). The national pharmaceuticals strategy report calls for further analysis on the impact and feasibility of maintaining a private payer role in a catastrophic drug coverage framework (Federal/Provincial/Territorial Ministerial Task Force, 2006). Some current discussions in this area include, e.g., Morgan et al. (2015), Daw et al. (2014) and Busby and Pedde (2014). Despite various recommendations, Canada is still the only country that does not provide universal coverage for prescription drugs among all developed countries with universal health care system. While many Canadian citizens and politicians believe that some form of universal drug coverage is needed, empirical evidence to inform the design of such a policy in the Canadian context is limited.1 In this study, we exploit the natural experiment of a policy change in the province of Quebec, Canada to evaluate whether and how a mandatory universal drug program affects drug insurance coverage, health care utilization and health outcomes. Quebec’s experience can provide valuable insights to inform policy debates regarding the optimal design of drug insurance in Canada and internationally. Using Canadian National Population Health Survey longitudinal data from 1994 to 2003, we find that the universal drug program increased drug insurance coverage by 33 percent and medication use by 13 percent. The latter estimate is in the middle range of those found in the Medicare Part D studies which vary from 5.9 percent (Yin et al., 2008) to 27 percent (Duggan and Scott-Morton, 2010) in drug utilization increase. To gauge the plausibility of the results, we calculated the elasticity of drug utilization. For simplicity we only take into account the reduction in co-payment rather than the whole non-linear pricing policy in the public plan. The coinsurance of the public plan is 25 percent, which implies a 75 percent reduction in out-of-pocket cost for those without insurance. The 13 percent increase in total drug utilization suggests an elasticity of approximately −0.17, which falls within the range of drug elasticity estimates from other contexts. Given that the utilization measure is total drug utilization, the elasticity for prescription drug utilization would be larger if there is substitution for non-prescription drugs because of the policy intervention. The estimated spillover effect on GP visits is about 10 percent but the policy has no statistically significant spillover effects on specialist visits and hospitalization. This provides evidence of a complementary relationship between prescription drugs and physician visits. The estimated effect on GP visits is large relative to zero or small spillover effects found in the U.S. context (Balkrishnan et al., 2001; Kaestner and Khan, 2012). This should not be unexpected given the multi-payer system for physician services in the U.S. in contrast to the free single-payer public system in Canada. Possible explanations for the finding of no effects on hospitalization include, first, that we look at the overall hospitalization rate rather than hospitalizations linked to pharmaceutical therapy and second that the hospital sector was downsizing and restructuring nationally in this period and the pharmaceutical effect was likely modest by comparison with the variation from those other sources. We find that health impacts of the policy are heterogeneous across the health outcome distribution, with large positive health gains concentrated among less healthy individuals. Analysis by pre-policy drug insurance status reveals that previously uninsured individuals experienced a large increase in the probability of taking any medication and visiting a general practitioner. Further analysis by the presence of chronic conditions shows that, compared to those without any chronic condition, the chronically ill experienced a much larger increase in the extensive margins of medication and general practitioner utilization. This paper makes several important contributions to the literature. First, it uses nationally representative longitudinal data to identify the impacts of a universal mandatory drug program by exploiting a natural experiment in Canada. Many previous studies use administrative or claims data for particular drug plans or specific population groups which limits generalizability of their findings. Moreover, the mandatory nature of the policy intervention creates a large exogenous variation in insurance coverage, in contrast to previous studies that focus on small changes in copayments. Second, this paper contributes to the literature by exploring the spillover effects of drug coverage on physician utilization and hospitalization. The limited empirical evidence of spillover effects is mixed and inconclusive. The context of universal public provision of physician and hospital services provides an extra advantage of identifying the spillover effects. Under health systems where physician and hospital services are covered by multiple insurers, such as the U.S. Medicare program, estimation of a uniform spillover effect may be complicated by the different cost-sharing structures of physician and hospital services across insurance plans. Third, this study adds to the literature by evaluating the impact of drug insurance on health outcomes and its impact in different parts of the health outcome distribution. Going beyond mean health effects, we analyze whether the policy effect is relatively larger among individuals with low health status versus high health status. To our knowledge, no other study has evaluated this type of heterogeneous health effects. Fourth, from a policy perspective, analysis of the drug program can help to inform the policy debate on expanding public drug coverage to universal level in Canada and internationally. The Quebec reform gives us a novel opportunity to examine the impacts of a policy that achieved universal drug coverage among the entire nonelderly population in Quebec. The mixed public and private financing structure of the Quebec program may also be useful for policymakers on general health insurance financing. For example, the individual mandate to buy prescription drug insurance in Quebec is similar to the individual mandate to obtain general health insurance of the U.S. national legislation passed in March 2010. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we provide background on previous work. Section 3 describes the institutional setting and policy change we are studying. In Section 4, we discuss our data and descriptive statistics. Empirical methods are discussed in Section 5. Section 6 gives the results of our analysis. Finally the conclusions are drawn in Section 7. 5. Empirical strategy We use a difference-in-differences (DD) approach to compare outcomes in Quebec versus other Canadian provinces. The pre-policy period includes the 1994/1995 and 1996/1997 cycles of the NPHS data and the post-policy period includes the three cycles from 1998/1999 to 2002/2003. The treatment group is the general population in Quebec before and after the policy change and the comparison group is the general population in the other provinces of Canada. We employ the following equation to estimate the impact of the reform on insurance coverage, health care utilization and health outcomes: $$ \begin{array} { r l } & { y _ { i p t } = f \left( \alpha + \delta _ { 1 } Q B _ { i } + \delta _ { 2 } \mathrm { P o s t } _ { t } + \beta ( \mathrm { P o s t } * Q B ) _ { i t } + \delta _ { 3 } \mathrm { O t h e r p r o v } _ { p } \right. } \\ & { \qquad \left. + \varphi \mathrm { Y e a r } _ { t } + \gamma X _ { i p t } + \varepsilon _ { i p t } \right) } \end{array} $$ where $y$ is an outcome variable for individual i in province $p$ at time t, QB is a dummy variable that takes the value of one for individual i in Quebec and zero for the other provinces, and Post takes the value of one for the years after 1997 and zero otherwise. The coefficient, $\beta$ , on the interaction term $( \mathrm { P o s t } ^ { * } Q B )$ gives the impact of the reform, i.e., the change in the outcome before and after the reform in Quebec relative to the other provinces after allowing for the same trend. Province and year dummies are included to control for province and year effects. Other independent variables $( X _ { i p t } )$ include age, sex, marital status, income, education and month of the interview in each survey cycle. In most of the specifications, individual fixed effects are added to control for unobserved individual heterogeneity to identify the policy effect using only the “withinindividual variation”. Detailed descriptions of the independent and dependent variables are shown in Appendix A. The key identifying assumption in the DD analysis is that the trends in the outcomes of Quebec and the other provinces would have been the same in the absence of the reform. In particular, we assume that the trends in all of the outcomes between Quebec and the other provinces would have been the same in the absence of the reform. There are several reasons to believe that the common trend assumption holds in our analysis. First, as we have mentioned in the institutional setting part, there are minimal drug insurance policy changes among the non-elderly population in the other provinces during our study period. Introduction of the Fair PharmaCare program in British Columbia in 2003 is at the very end of our study period. Second, the institutional context of physician and hospital services is similar across provinces within Canada. All provinces and territories provide universal coverage for medically necessary hospital and physician services that are free at the point of use. Most hospitals are private, not-for-profit organizations funded through global budget. Although there is the introduction and subsequent removal of physician global budgets across a number of the provinces during our study period, these payment changes reforms would likely have reduced use of physician services and biased our estimates downward. The majority of physicians are remunerated by fee for service during our study period 1994 to 2003. Our study period is prior to the primary care reforms in Ontario, Alberta, British Columbia and Quebec. Actually, there has been little changes in the primary care sector at the system level until the early 2000s (Hutchison et al., 2011). Real transformative changes in the Ontario primary care sector actually happened around the mid 2000s. Third, graphical evidence in the figures show similar trends in the outcomes in Quebec and the rest of Canada. Similarities in summary statistics in Table II suggest that the other provinces serve as a good comparison group. Falsification tests and various model specifications will be conducted to test the identifying assumption and check the robustness of our estimates.

The estimate of the impact on drug utilization is in the middle range of those found in the Medicare Part D studies which vary from 5.9 percent (Yin et al., 2008) to 27 percent (Duggan and Scott-Morton, 2010). Given that the utilization measure is total drug utilization, the elasticity for prescription drug utilization would be larger if there is substitution for non-prescription drugs because of the policy intervention. The estimated effects on GP visits are large relative to zero or small spillover effects found in the U.S. context (Balkrishnan et al., 2001; Kaestner and Khan, 2012). This should not be unexpected given that physician services are free in the Canadian context while the multi-payer system in the U.S. varies in co-payment for physician visits across insurance plans. Panel B of Table IV reports the linear probability regression results for all indicator variables of utilization.22 In both the OLS and fixed effects linear models, coefficient estimates of the policy effects are still very similar in the base model and the model with individual control variables. The mandatory drug program led to an increase in the probability of any medication use in the previous month by 2.2 to 3.2 percentage points. The likelihood of visiting a GP increased by about 2 percentage points although not statistically significant in the fixed effects models. There was little effect on the likelihood of visiting a specialist. Finally both OLS and fixed effects models failed to reveal any statistically significant effects on the likelihood of having an inpatient admission in the previous year. Panel C of Table IV presents the estimated impact of the mandatory drug program on health status. The program had a small positive effect on self-assessed health status and HUI. Previous studies document that an increase of 0.03 or greater in HUI score is considered as clinically important, and an increase of 0.01 is generally important (Horsman et al., 2003; Grootendorst et al., 2000). The estimated impact on HUI is around 0.010, representing an important improvement in health status. Our preferred specification is fixed effects Poisson and fixed effects linear models which provide more conservative estimates than those without fixed effects. Therefore, we will focus on the fixed effects Poisson and fixed effects linear models in what follows. The graphical evidence in Figs. 2, 3, 7 and 8 indicates that the large policy impacts lagged one period relative to the immediate increase in drug coverage after the policy.23 There are some possible explanations to this. First, it takes time for people to adapt to the new policy. Moreover, eligible Quebec residents are required to register for the public plan before it takes effects. Second, physicians, pharmacists and, especially, private insurance companies, also need time to adjust. The physician shortage situation in Quebec in the 1990s also likely made the adjustment slower. We explore the dynamic effects of the policy change in Appendix B and find that the impacts on most of the outcome variables grow larger over time. Overall, the results suggest substantially larger adjustments in drug consumption and GP utilization in the long than short term. We have shown a reduced form impact of the policy on utilization and health outcomes. If we assume that the policy only affected the reduced form outcomes through the expansion of drug insurance coverage, we can estimate the impact of drug insurance coverage on the outcomes. (The assumption can be violated sometimes; for example, if the contents of the coverage are also changed). Combining the results in Tables III and IV, a one percentage point increase in drug insurance coverage increased medication use in the past month by 0.6 (13/21) percent and annual GP visits by 0.5 (10/21) percent in the population. For the extensive margin, a one percentage point increase in drug insurance coverage increased the probability of any medication use in the previous month by 0.10 (2.2/21) to 0.15 (3.2/21) percentage points in the population. A one percentage point increase in drug insurance coverage increased HUI by 0.0003 in the population. Given that the insurance coverage in the other provinces is 64 percent, we will expect a 22 percent increase in medication use and 18 percent increase in GP visits if all of the other provinces intend to introduce a similar drug plan to cover the 36 percent uninsured. 6.2. Heterogeneous effects at different points of the HUI distribution DD conditional quantile regression estimates by deciles of HUI are plotted in Fig. 9. We find that the impact on health is monotonically decreasing and is virtually zero from the median to the ninth decile. This finding should not be surprising given that more than 50 percent of the population in the sample have HUI greater than 0.97. It should be noted that the positive impact on HUI is 0.038 at the first decile, representing a clinically important improvement in health status. At the 20th and 30th percentiles, the policy effects are around 0.015 and 0.014 and still statistically significant. These results suggest that it is mainly less healthy individuals that experienced an improvement in health status, indicating that high value pharmaceutical drugs may be under-used among them. Therefore, offering affordable pharmaceutical drugs to these high risk people can improve their health substantially. For policy purposes, this finding is crucial since a mandatory drug program can generate substantial health gains for those with worse health outcomes, who are usually the target of public drug programs. It provides useful information for policymakers who are considering a national pharmacare program in the Canadian context and for optimal drug insurance design in general. 6.3. Subgroup analysis by drug insurance status and chronic condition One important consideration in understanding the potential effects of the universal drug policy is how it may differentially affect sub-populations. If patients in different subgroups tend to use different combinations of inputs, such as medications, physician and hospital services, to produce health and if health care is more effective for some patients than others, then the benefits of health insurance should vary accordingly. Thanks to the panel nature of the data, individuals who were previously uninsured can be identified and subgroup analysis by previous insurance status is conducted to further identify the heterogeneous impacts of the policy. Similarly, policy effects by chronic condition are estimated. We examine the heterogeneous effects by looking at the interactions between these subgroups and the main treatment variable. Table V presents the estimation results from fixed effects Poisson and fixed effects linear probability models, including interactions between the treatment variable and individual’s pre-policy drug insurance status. Panel A presents results of drug and physician utilization, Panel B results of the probability of any medication use, a physician visit and hospitalization, and Panel C results of health status. In Panel A, we continue to find evidence of positive policy effects on medication use and GP visits. The effects on medication use are slightly larger for the previously uninsured, but the differences are not statistically significant. The differential effects on GP utilization for the previously insured and uninsured are also not statistically different from zero. We also find large positive effects on specialist visits, with the effects much larger for the previously uninsured, however, none of the estimates are statistically significant. In Panel B, the coefficients of the pre-policy insurance status interactions suggest that the positive effects on the probability of taking medications or visiting a GP are larger for the previously uninsured. We find no evidence of policy effects on the probability of specialist visit and hospitalization. As is shown in column 1 of Panel C, the coefficient on the interaction term suggests that the policy impact on the HUI for the previously uninsured is much smaller than the previously insured. An $F$ test $F .$ -statistic $= 0 . 7 1$ , $p$ -value $= 0 . 4 0$ ) shows that the HUI effects for the previously uninsured are not jointly statistically different from zero. Results in column 2 of Panel C reveal that the previously uninsured are more likely to report excellent or very good health after the policy change but the estimates are not statistically significant. It is surprising that the results in Table V seem to show that the policy had a large drug utilization impact for the previously insured. However, there are several possible explanations for this. First, this policy required private insurers to have the same level of coverage standard (i.e., drug formulary) as the public plan. Private plans could be more generous than the public plan but not less. Some of the previously insured may increase their utilization as their coverage became more generous. Second, a new public program can stimulate demand on all fronts. It may make people, the previously insured in particular, aware of their drug coverage and ask their doctors to prescribe more for them (Commissaire à La Santé et au Bien-Être, 2015). Finally, the introduction of a large public drug plan may change the market structure of the private drug insurance industry. For example, some evidence suggests that the introduction of Medicare Part D plans led to a large reduction in prices for brand-name prescription drugs with close substitutes (Duggan and Scott-Morton, 2010). If this is the case with the Quebec drug insurance market, the previously insured may possibly increase their utilization. Accordingly, the effects on GP utilization are also large among the previously insured because of the complementary relationship between medication use and GP visits. We further examine the impacts of the policy at different points of the utilization distribution among the previously uninsured and insured. We estimated fixed effects linear probability models (similar to those in columns 1 and 2 in Panel B of Table V), where the dependent variable is an indicator of individuals exceeding specific medication use or physician visit cutoffs (e.g., indicators of using more than two medications, more than three medications etc.). We find that the increase in drug utilization for the previously insured is concentrated at the intensive margin, in contrast to the previously uninsured. Accordingly GP utilization for the previously insured is concentrated at the high end of the distribution, in contrast to the previously uninsured at the low end of the distribution. This seems to imply that there are some changes in the private plan coverage or awareness of it.

Sensitivity and robustness analysis We can test the identifying assumption of our DD estimation by falsification (placebo) tests for the years before the policy change. We define 1994/1995 as the pre-policy years and 1996/1997 as the post-policy year in the falsification tests. The test results (shown in Table VII) suggest that none of the coefficients is statistically significant except the coefficient in one of the specialist utilization models, which is significantly negative. Of course, out of 18 coefficient estimates (even if the variables were random numbers) it would be unusual not to have at least one that is statistically significant at the five or ten percent levels. Overall, the falsification tests do not reject the common trend hypothesis in our models. We further estimated full dynamic models by adding all interactions of Quebec and time dummies.25 The results are shown in Appendix B. We find that all coefficients on the interaction of Quebec and year 1994 (two periods before the policy change) are close to zero. Again this indicates that other provinces exhibited a parallel trend to Quebec in all of the outcomes. (Please refer to Appendix B for details). A number of recent papers have raised concerns about inference in DD estimation (Bertrand et al., 2004; Donald and Lang, 2007; Cameron et al., 2008). The main problem is that the standard errors computed by conventional estimation methods are too small if the error term in the estimating equation includes unobserved groupyear effects (Especially, the errors are serially correlated within groups, leading to inflated t-statistics if this is ignored). To address this serial correlation issue, we compare the standard errors clustered at the province level and individual level. We find that in most cases the standard errors are larger when clustered at the individual level, therefore, we report our main results with standard errors clustered at the individual level. For the Poisson models with individual-specific effects, we report the bootstrapped standard errors.

Several other specifications were estimated to check the robustness of our estimates. As described in Appendix A, all the medication and physician utilization variables are truncated at the 99.5 percentiles. We tried the original values without truncation and the estimates are larger and more significant than those in Table IV. The results are essentially unchanged when we truncate them at the 99th percentiles. Further, including health status, such as self-assessed health status or chronic condition status, as control variables in the utilization equations does not change the estimates substantially. Controlling for initial health status in the first cycle of the survey also makes little difference to our estimates. It may be possible that access to specialists is different from access to GPs, who act as gatekeepers in the health care system, so we included an indicator variable for whether the respondent has a regular family doctor or not in the specialist visit equation. However, there is no meaningful difference in the estimates. 7. Conclusion and discussion Canada continues to debate the merits of introducing a national pharmacare program. The debate needs to be informed by evidence regarding the effectiveness of expanded drug insurance coverage. This study examines the impact of Quebec’s mandatory universal drug program on insurance coverage, health care utilization and health outcomes. We find that the introduction of the mandatory drug program substantially increased drug coverage among the general population. The program also increased medication use and GP visits. No statistically significant effects were found for specialist visits and hospitalization. Our subgroup analysis by pre-reform drug insurance status suggests that the reform had no differential impacts on total drug and GP utilization among the previously insured and uninsured. Furthermore, effects on drug and GP utilization for the previously uninsured are concentrated at the extensive margin, indicating that the reform improved access to these services for them. Subgroup analysis by presence of chronic condition reveals that the reform had a much large effect on the probability of GP visit for those with chronic conditions. Most importantly, results of quantile regressions show that the reform had differential health impacts. People with worse health outcomes experienced a large improvement in their health status. Our findings are consistent with most previous studies showing that individuals increase medication use if they have drug insurance. Our estimates of the policy impacts on drug insurance coverage and drug utilization are comparable to those from the existing Medicare Part D studies. This should not be unexpected because the Quebec program and Part D share many similarities. Our finding of a strong positive spillover effect on physician visits is consistent with some previous studies (e.g., Winkelmann, 2004) but in contrast to some Medicare Part D studies reporting zero or small positive spillover effects in the U.S. context (Balkrishnan et al., 2001; Kaestner and Khan, 2012). This implies that the magnitudes of the spillover effects may depend on the institutional context for physician service financing. Our finding of heterogeneous health impacts at different parts of the health distribution provides useful information to understand the link between drug insurance and health status. Previous evidence of no or positive health effects of drug coverage is possibly due to the differences in the health status of the study population. The findings provide useful information for the implementation of a universal pharmacare program in a public health system. A public drug program covering those who do not have private drug plans can improve access to medications, increase GP visits, and generate substantial health gains for the chronically ill and less healthy people. In the long run, this may lead to reduction in overall health care utilization. The mixed public and private program provides a feasible solution to the design of a national pharmacare program. Given public concerns about the cost of a pure public drug program and the status quo of private insurance industries, the incremental change of adding a public drug plan on top of the private plans is promising. The positive spillover effects on physician visits, which are free in Canada, can also shed light on the policy concern that private drug insurance contributes to the pro-rich inequity in physician utilization (Allin and Hurley, 2009). Offering drug insurance coverage to the low income people, who are less likely to have private drug insurance, may help to reduce such pro-rich inequity. Future research can build on this study in several ways. For example, we have examined the impact of the drug program on health care utilization and health outcomes; future research can explore the impact on out-of-pocket drug expenditure and total drug expenditure. In addition, if there are data for prescription and non-prescription drug utilization, the policy impact on the substitution between them is another interesting research question.

Vorwort
Auf den ersten Blick präsentiert sich die Operationsforschung (Operations Research) als eine Sammlung wertvoller Verfahrenstechniken, mit deren Hilfe gewisse Führungsprobleme in optimaler Weise gelöst werden können.
Der lediglich an den mathematisch-statistischen Aspekten Interessierte mag sich damit begnügen; der theoretisch interessierte Betriebswirtschafter, aber auch der Unternehmer, der die Absicht hat, eine Operations-Research-Abteilung in seiner Unternehmung zu errichten, werden sich intensiver mit der neuen Disziplin zu beschäftigen haben. Denn beide wollen etwas über die Anwendungsmöglichkeiten und Grenzen der neuen Rechentechniken wissen.
Sie werden bald feststellen, da die Operationsforschung vor allem methodologisch bedeutsam ist. In der Tat hat die Operationsforschung die latente verfahrenstheoretische Auseinandersetzung in der Betriebswirtschaftslehre und darüber hinaus in der gesamten Wirtschaftstheorie neu entflammt.
Ihre unbestreitbaren Erfolge in bestimmten Funktionsbereichen der Wirtschaft haben ihre Befürworter in der Auffassung bestärkt, daB die naturwissenschaftlich-kalkülsprachliche Forschungsmethode die der Betriebswirtschaftslehre adäquate Methode sei. Sie konnten jedoch andererseits das Unbehagen jener Betriebswirtschafter nicht beseitigen, die, obwohl sie bereit sind, den Wert der neuen Verfahren für die Lösung begrenzter Aufgaben anzuerkennen, die These ablehnen, da nur die numerische Methode der Betriebswirtschaftslehre entspreche. Diese Betriebswirtschafter weisen die Auffassung zurück, da der Betrieb ein servomechanistisches System sei, zwischen dessen Organisationselementen (Menschen, Maschinen, Material) kausalmechanische Abläufe bestehen. Sie betrachten die mechanistische Auffassung des Betriebs nicht als eine Höherentwicklung, sondern als eine bedauernswerte, ja nicht selten als eine gefährliche Fehlentwicklung und ereifern sich nur deshalb nicht mehr, weil sie überzeugt davon sind, daB die neuen Verfahren - sofern sie auf höhere Führungsentscheidungen angewendet werden - ohnehin nur in Hörsälen und Studierstuben gedeihen und sich bei der praktischen Bewährung im Leben als unanwendbar erweisen werden.
Der Streit ist an sich nicht neu. Er ist nur die Fortsetzung jener Auseinandersetzung, welche ,mathematische" und ,,nichtmathematische" Betriebswirtschafter seit langem führen. Aber dieses Mal ist ein neues Element hinzugekommen.
Früher waren nämlich die Betriebswirtschafter gewissermaBen unter sich; mit der Operationsforschung haben sich jedoch die Fachmathematiker und Fachstatistiker selbst zu Wort gemeldet und nehmen aktiven Anteil an der Diskussion.
Die Konfrontierung der Operationsforschung mit der Betriebswirtschaftslehre ist mehr als nur eine Untersuchung, ob neue, bisher unbekannte Rechentechniken für die Lösung bestimmter betrieblicher Aufgaben brauchbar oder unbrauchbar sind. Es geht um Wesentlicheres. Vom Ergebnis dieses Verfahrensstreites wird nämlich sowohl die Gestaltung der Lehre auf den Hochschulen als auch die Gestaltung des Lebens in den Betrieben abhängen. Letzten Endes geht es um das grundsätzliche Problem, ob sich die traditionelle Betriebswirtschaftslehre zu einer informationswissenschaftlich orientierten, logistischen Systemforschung, zu einer katallaktisch-abstrakten Leistungsgröβenlehre entwickelt oder ob sie ihren tragenden Begriff der indeterminierten Leistung beibehält, eine morphologisch-anschauliche Leistungslehre schafft und daher auch nicht in eine Betriebskybernetik, sondern in eine neu zu begründende, die Willensfreiheit der Wirtschaftssubjekte berücksichtigende Betriebswirtschaftspolitik mündet.
Das Wertvolle an der Operationsforschung sind also nicht nur die neuen mathematisch-statistischen Verfahren, sondern auch und insbesondere die Tatsache, da sie den Betriebswirtschafter wieder an die philosophischen Grundlagen seiner Wissenschaft heranbringt.
Genf, im Januar 1963

I. Die Problemstellung
Die Operations Research ist als militärische Operationsforschung während des zweiten Weltkrieges in Europa, und zwar in GroBbritannien, entstanden. Sie wurde von amerikanischen Wissenschaftlern übernommen, in den Vereinigten Staaten weiterentwickelt und kam von dort in modifizierter Form wieder nach Europa zurück. Hier hatte man sie in der Zwischenzeit zwar nicht vergessen, sie war in GroBbritannien sogar sehr bald auf wirtschaftliche Probleme ausgedehnt worden, hatte aber keine weitere geographische Ausbreitung gefunden.
Während die originäre Operations Research einen rein militärischen Charakter hatte, war die in den ersten Nachkriegsjahren gepflegte Operationsforschung längst schon über den militärischen Rahmen hinausgewachsen und zu einem Forschungsgebiet der technischen Wissenschaften und der Wirtschaftswissenschaft geworden. Nicht mehr die wissenschaftliche Behandlung des Kampfeinsatzes von Mensch und Material stand im Vordergrund des Interesses, sondern die wirtschaftliche Aktivität des Menschen.
Die Anwendung der Operationsforschung auf wirtschaftliche Probleme war also das neue Anliegen. Durch diesen Themawechsel machte die Operationsforschung auch im deutschsprachigen Mitteleuropa auf sich aufmerksam. In der Zwischenzeit hatte sie sich als recherche operationelle in Frankreich und als ricerca operativa auch in Italien durchgesetzt und war zu einer anerkannten wissenschaftlichen Disziplin geworden. Im deutschsprachigen Raum ging die Entwicklung langsamer vor sich; wohl - wie man jetzt nach gründlicheren Untersuchungen des Wesens der Operationsforschung sagen kann - deshalb, weil hier eine ausgebildete Betriebswirtschaftslehre bestand, die längst schon zu all den Problemen der Unternehmungsführung, denen sich auch die Operationsforschung zuwendet, Stellung genommen hatte. Es bestand also keine dringende Veranlassung, neue, noch unbewährte Methoden und Ratschläge zu übernehmen. Langsam, dann allmählich auch schneller breitete sich das Gedankengut der Operations Research aus, und schlielich bezeichnete Käfer die Operationsforschung in einem Vortrag auf der Universität Mainz als jüngsten SproB der Betriebswirtschaftslehre, und Frenckner forderte die betriebswirtschaftliche Forschung und Praxis auf, die operationsanalytischen Methoden ,,möglichst unverzüglich" zu übernehmen, da sich ,eine Kombination dieser Methoden mit den traditionellen Forschungsmethoden der Betriebswirtschaftslehre als sehr vorteilhaft" erweise (1). Damit war sie in die betriebswirtschaftliche Diskussion eingetreten und forderte zu einer Stellungnahme heraus.
Die Betriebswirtschaftslehre sieht sich also der neuen Operationsforschung gegenüber und mu in irgendeiner Weise zu ihr Stellung nehmen. Sie kann sie ablehnen oder vorbehaltlos akzeptieren; auf jeden Fall mu sie diese neue Form der wissenschaftlichen Forschung auf betrieblicher Ebene zur Kenntnis nehmen. Wird doch behauptet, dab mit Hilfe der neuen Verfahren optimale Lösungen gefunden werden können, die mit den bisherigen betriebswirtschaftlichen Verfahren nicht erreichbar waren (2), ja noch mehr, daB die betriebswirtschaftliche Forschung durch neue, insbesondere von der Statistik her angeregte Erkenntnismethoden und durch die Einsatzmöglichkeit von Datenverarbeitungsmaschinen grundlegend reformiert werde (3). Illetschko fordert, da es alsobald innerhalb der Betriebswirtschaftslehre gelingen müsse, die neuartigen Rechentechniken neben den alten, überkommenen als technische Verfahren ,ebenso lehrbar und auffabar zu gestalten, wie ihr das auf dem konventionellen Gebiet der Bilanzrechnung, der Kostenrechnung, der Preiskalkulation usw. gelungen ist" (4). Manche Autoren sprechen sogar von einem Wendepunkt in der Betriebsführung und stellen damit Behauptungen auf, die für die Betriebswirtschaftslehre von essentieller Bedeutung sind (5). Einige sind sogar der Meinung, da man überhaupt erst, seitdem die Betriebsführung ,,Operations Research" als Mittel zur Lösung von Betriebsproblemen anwendet, von einer wissenschaftlichen Betriebsführung sprechen könne (6), und in der Harvard Business Review kann man lesen, daB es sich bei dem linearen Programmieren, der vermutlich bedeutendsten Verfahrenstechnik der Operationsforschung, ,um den markantesten betriebswirtschaftlichen Fortschritt seit der Erfindung der doppelten Buchführung im Mittelalter handele" (7).
In Amerika heiBt es: "Operations research brings something vital and new to the American management science" (8), und im deutschsprachigen Mitteleuropa wird vorausgesagt, dab ,die Lehre von den Operations Research ... - was sie in Amerika bereits ist — wohl auch bei uns zu einer wichtigen neuen Disziplin der Betriebswirtschaftslehre werden" (9) wird. Böhm behauptet, daB es sich bei den neuen Verfahren um eine der interessantesten Entwicklungen der letzten Jahrzehnte handele; die Neuerungen seien nicht nur für die Unternehmungsplanung, sondern auch für die Entwicklung der Wirtschaftstheorie der kauf.. männischen Unternehmung gleichmäBig bedeutsam, und deren Ausstrahlungen würden uns alle in den nächsten Jahren noch zunehmend beschäftigen (10).
Mit der Formulierung der Operationsforschung als der höchsten Stufe des betrieblichen Rechnungswesens schlieBlich wurde erreicht, daB sich der Kreis der interessierten Betriebswirtschafter erweiterte, denn das Rechnungswesen war die Domäne vieler Betriebswirte und hatte seit Jahrzehnten eine Zentralstellung in der Betriebswirtschaftslehre inne. Die Reaktion war verständlich, denn die Behauptung, daB die Operationsforschung die höchste Stufe des Rechnungswesens sei, schloB ja bis zu einem gewissen Grade ein Werturteil ein.
Mit einem Male waren die Buchhaltung, die Kostenrechnung einschlieBlich der Plankostenrechnung, ja selbst die Kennzahlenrechnung, die bisherige Betriebsstatistik, die Budgetrechnung und wie man die einzelnen Sachgebiete des betrieblichen Rechnungswesens noch einteilen will, degradiert. Sie waren nur noch traditionell, konventionell und muten es sich gefallen lassen, in ihrer dominierenden Bedeutung für die Unternehmungsführung von der strategischen Operationsforschung abgelöst zu werden.
Dieser Situation sehen wir uns heute gegenüber. Und aus dieser Lage heraus entstand das Thema dieser Arbeit: Kritik der betriebswirtschaftlichen Operationsforschung (Operations Research). Die Arbeit will die Operations Research der Betriebswirtschaftslehre gegenüberstellen und untersuchen, was neu ist und was bereits zum Bestand der Betriebswirtschaftslehre gehört. Darüber hinaus will sie aber auch kritisch sein, d. h. prüfen, ob das Neue dazu beiträgt, das betriebswirtschaftliche Wissen zu bereichern. Denn etwas Neues muB nicht notwendigerweise brauchbar sein, und möge es sich in anderen Lebensbereichen des Menschen, wie z. B. in der Technik, den Naturwissenschaften, dem Militär usw., noch so bewährt haben.
Es wird in dieser Arbeit nicht nur die Operations Research schlechthin analysiert, sondern auch und hauptsächlich jene, die sich auf wirtschaftliche Tätigkeiten bezieht, also die betriebswirtschaftliche Operationsforschung. Die Konfrontation der beiden Forschungsgebiete ist gerechtfertigt, weil beide den Betrieb und das Leben in ihm zum Gegenstand haben; ja die Parallelität der Forschungsaufgaben ist manchmal so verblüffend, daB man geneigt ist, die Operationsforschung mit der Betriebswirtschaftslehre gleichzusetzen, um dann allerdings sofort wieder die Unterschiede herauszustellen.
Aus dem in gleicher Weise interessierenden Objekt, nämlich dem Betrieb, leitet der Betriebswirt auch seine Legitimation zur Behandlung der Operationsforschung ab. Diese Feststellung mag etwas überraschend sein; wenn man aber in der Literatur auf die so oft genannte Team-Arbeit in der Operationsforschung stöBt, wird man Mathematiker, Statistiker, Soziologen, Nationalökonomen, Psychologen, Arzte, Physiker, Astronomen usw. finden, meistens aber vergeblich einen Betriebswirt suchen. Das ist befremdend und dürfte wohl auch der Grund dafür sein, daB sich die Arbeit beider Sachgebiete bisher im Grunde genommen nebeneinander und ohne zu groBe Berücksichtigung des anderen bewegt hat. Dieser Zustand ist aber auf die Dauer untragbar. Die Betriebswirtschaftslehre braucht die Operationsforschung, aber ebenso braucht umgekehrt die betriebswirtschaftliche Operationsforschung auch die Betriebswirtschaftslehre, wenn sie nicht eine wirklichkeitsfremde Zahlenspielerei werden will. Bevor dieses Nebeneinander aber beseitigt werden kann, ist es notwendig, zu klären, welche Beziehungen, Gemeinsamkeiten und inakzeptablen Unterschiede zwischen der Betriebswirtschaftslehre und der Operationsforschung bestehen. Dann erst werden die Möglichkeiten und Grenzen der Operationsforschung im Rahmen der Betriebswirtschaftslehre bestimmt werden können, und allmählich wird sich dann durch die Arbeiten vieler der wissenschaftliche Standort der beiden Disziplinen klären. Die Betriebswirtschaftslehre hat die Pficht, gleichgültig, was sie von der Operationsforschung hält, sich mit dieser auseinanderzusetzen. Mag der Anwendungsbereich in der Wirtschaftswissenschaft auch enger sein als in den Naturwissenschaften, so entbindet das die Betriebswirtschaftslehre als Wissenschaft aber nicht von ihrer Verpflichtung, die Anwendungsmöglichkeiten zu erforschen.
Der Verfasser dieser Arbeit unternimmt seinen Teil der Aufgabe. Er geht dabei von einer Betriebswirtschaftslehre aus, in deren Mittelpunkt die Leistung steht — die Leistung, die Funktion, die von einer Person gesetzt wird und die dem selbsttätigen Ablauf des betrieblichen Geschehens entgegengesetzt ist. Sein Standort ist also eine funktionale Betriebswirtschaftslehre im Sinne einer leistungsorientierten Betriebswirtschaftslehre. Der Hinweis darauf, daB mit der funktionalen Lehre eine auf die Leistung abgestellte Theorie gemeint sei, scheint deshalb von groBer Bedeutung zu sein, weil mit dem Aufkommen der mathematischen Verfahren in der betriebswirtschaftlichen Theorie unter einer funktionalen Betriebswirtschaftslehre etwas ganz anderes verstanden wird. Die mathematische Betriebswirtschaftslehre versteht, ausgehend von der Produktionsfaktorenlehre und von der Produktionsfunktion, unter der funktionalen Betriebswirtschaftslehre oder, wie sie auch genannt wird, der funktionellen Richtung der Betriebswirtschaftslehre (Waffenschmidt) jene, deren Zentralbegriff nicht die Leistung, sondern der mathematische Funktionsbegriff ist.
Selbstverständlich mu man sich darüber im klaren sein, daB die funktionale, leistungsorientierte Betriebswirtschaftslehre in dem angeführten Sinne, um mit Gutenberg (11) zu reden,nur ein systematischer Ansatz unter vielen möglichen" ist, doch ist die Bestimmung einer Position für jede wirtschaftswissenschaftliche Analyse unerläBlich und eine Kritik schlieBlich ohne eigenen wissenschaftlichen Standort überhaupt unmöglich. Eine bloBe Aufzählung von Tatsachen würde zwar dem Leser eine Vorstellung von dem Wesen der Operationsforschung und den einzelnen operationsanalytischen Verfahrenstechniken geben, könnte jedoch niemals die Beziehungen zwischen den beiden Disziplinen — und darauf kommt es in der vorliegenden Arbeit an - aufdecken.
Noch aus einem anderen Grunde ist die Festlegung des wissenschaftlichen Standortes von eminenter Bedeutung: Mit der Auffassung vom Wesen der Betriebswirtschaftslehre ist nämlich auch gleichzeitig das Verfahren bestimmt, und dieses ist für eine verfahrenstheoretische Analyse, welche diese Arbeit in vielen entscheidenden Teilen ist, von ausschlaggebender Bedeutung.
Für die Klärung des Problems erscheint es nicht erforderlich, eine Vielzahl von Spezialfällen anzuführen; soweit es notwendig ist, werden Beispiele angeführt, und im übrigen wird auf die Einzelpublikationen hingewiesen, die so zahlreich geworden sind, daB bereits Bibliographien über die Operationsforschung erscheinen konnten.
Eine Bewältigung der Materie ist ohne Studium der angelsächsischen Literatur auf diesem Gebiete kaum möglich.
II. Die Definition der Operations Research
Der englische Begriff ,,Operations Research" deckt einen Vorstellungsinhalt, den man wohl sehr gut im Deutschen umschreiben kann, für den man aber immer noch keine zutreffende Übersetzung gefunden hat. Offensichtlich ist unter dem Begriffsbestandteil ,,operation" (die Briten verwenden den Ausdruck ,,Operational") eine durch eine Person gesetzte Handlung, Aktion, zu verstehen. Im Englischen dürfte die Entscheidung für die Verwendung des Ausdruckes ,Operation" und nicht etwa für ",action" oder ,performance" auf den militärischen Ursprung der Operations Research zurückzuführen sein.
Es handelt sich bei der Operation um eine abgegrenzte Tätigkeit, die - wie dem zweiten Begriffsbestandteil entnommen werden kann — wissenschaftlich analysiert werden soll.
1. Sprachliche Schwierigkeiten bei der Übersetzung
Aber damit war der englische Ausdruck noch nicht eindeutig durch einen deutschen Begriff präzisiert, und hier begannen die Schwierigkeiten. Fast eine jede Arbeit, die sich mit der Operationsforschung beschäftigt, setzt sich mit dem Begriff auseinander, und der jeweilige Autor schlieBt sich entweder irgendeiner bestehenden Ubersetzung an oder prägt einen neuen Begriff. Man sollte dieses Schaffen neuer Wörter nicht als eine Sucht nach Originalität auslegen, sondern eher als ein Ringen nach dem Richtigen. Das beweisen alle Publikationen, deren Autoren offensichtlich redlich bemüht sind, einen Begriff zu formulieren, der allen Anforderungen entspricht. Bis heute hat sich aber eine allgemein anerkannte deutsche Ubersetzung noch nicht durchgesetzt.
Die Definition eines Begriffs ist von gröBter methodologischer Bedeutung, und man sollte sich nicht zu leichtfertig jener Meinung anschlieBen, die besagt, da es gleichgültig sei, wie man die Operations Research definiere, und es nur darauf ankomme, daB sich jeder darunter etwas vorstellen könne. ,Hinter der Unsicherheit der Namensgebung verbirgt sich der Mangel eines klar erkannten und klar herausgestellten Erkenntnisobjektes", sagt Schönpflug, und es ist ihm diesbezüglich vollinhaltlich zuzustimmen (1). Man kann eben mit einem solchen Begriff wissenschaftlich nicht arbeiten, und wenn die Operations Research nicht als Modeausdruck, als ein ,New-Look" betrachtet werden will, muB sie definiert werden. Aus dem Begriff leiten sich die Methoden ab, kann eine wissenschaftliche Disziplin oder ein Teilgebiet überhaupt erst aufgebaut werden, und ohne definierten Begriff kann das Verhältnis zu anderen Wissenschaften, hier das Verhältnis zwischen Operations Research und Betriebswirtschaftslehre, gar nicht bestimmt werden. Will man nicht in der bloBen Deskription unzusammenhängender Sachverhalte verbleiben, so muB man vom Begriff ausgehen. Da dic Definition nur die sprachliche Form des Vorstellungsinhaltes ist, muB die Beschäftigung mit ihr gleichzeitig alles über den Inhalt aussagen, und indem man so vorgeht, ist auch gewährleistet, daB die Lücken ihrer unvollständigen oder unrichtigen Definition gefunden werden.
Im allgemeinen sind angelsächsische Autoren weniger an Definitionen interessiert als deutschsprachige. Bezeichnend hierfür ist etwa die Stellungnahme Pococks, für den die Definition neuer Tätigkeitsbereiche im allgemeinen kein fruchtbares Gebiet für Diskussionen ist (2); andererseits findet man in der amerikanischen Literatur auch Vertreter der Operationsforschung, die den Wert einer genauen Definition sehr wohl kennen und in ihren Untersuchungen der Definierung einen breiten Raum widmen. An erster Stelle dürfte hier Morse zu nennen sein, der u. a. feststellt, daB die Operationsforschung auch deshalb genau umschrieben werden müsse, weil die Wissenschaftler benachbarter Gebiete wissen wollen, wodurch sich die Operationsforschung von ihrem eigenen Wissensgebiet unterscheidet (3).
Aus dem britischen ,,Operational Research" wurde das amerikanische ,Operations Research". Im deutschen Sprachgebiet arbeitete man zunächst mit dem Ausdruck ,Ablaufs- und Planungsforschung", ist jedoch in letzter Zeit dazu übergegangen, dem Begriff Verfahrensforschung den Vorrang zu geben. Für die Verwendung des Wortes ,Verfahrensforschung" haben sich Kosiol, Käfer, Henzel, Wittmann, Meier-Billeter und Frenckner eingesetzt (4).
Käfer lehnt den Ausdruck Ablaufsforschung deshalb ab, weil er zu passiv ist; er weist damit zweifellos auf einen wahren Sachverhalt hin, der im übrigen in den nachfolgenden Abschnitten noch ausführlicher behandelt wird. Er sagt ferner, daB die in Österreich eingeführte Ubersetzung ,Unternehmensforschung" miBverständlich sei, und gibt damit wohl die Meinung zahlreicher anderer Betriebswirte wieder. Denn in der betriebswirtschaftlichen Diskussion steht das Begriffspaar Betrieb und Unternehmung im Mittelpunkt vieler wissenschaftlicher Auseinandersetzungen und hat dazu geführt, daB mit dem Worte ,,Unternehmung" bzw. ,Unternehmen" eine ganz bestimmte Vorstellung assoziiert wird, nämlich die Vorstellung des rechtlichen Rahmens des Betriebes oder allgemeiner auch des mehrere Betriebe umfassenden Gebildes. Freilich verstehen Sagoroff und Adam, die den Ausdruck ,Unternehmensforschung" eingeführt haben, unter einem Unternehmen nicht nur eine wirtschaftliche Aktion, sondern auch Mabnahmen in anderen Bereichen menschlicher Tätigkeit, ,,so etwa auch Seuchen- und Schädlingsbekämpfung, Kriegsführung usw.". Ihr Ausdruck ,Unternehmen" hat nichts mit dem morphologischen Begriff der Betriebswirtschaftslehre zu tun; ,Unternehmen" ist für sie die menschliche Aktivität im Sinne von Aktionen, Operationen und Prozessen schlechthin (5). Sie kommen nicht aus der Betriebswirtschaftslehre, sondern haben die neuen Verfahrenstechniken unmittelbar aus der angelsächsischen Literatur übernommen und damit auch den Begriff so übersetzt, wie es dem englischen bzw. amerikanischen Vorstellungsinhalt entspricht. Der Ubersetzung des Wortes ,Operation" mit ,Unternehmen" steht an und für sich nichts im Wege, besonders dann nicht, wenn, wie das bei Sagoroff und Adam zweifellos der Fall ist, eine klare Definition beigegeben wird; wendet man aber die Operations Research auf betriebswirtschaftliche Probleme an, dann wird man aus dem angeführten Grunde vorteilhafterweise mit einem anderen Ausdruck arbeiten.
Die Ubersetzung mit ,,Planungsforschung" ist verständlich, wenn man bedenkt, daB die Operations Research, wie ebenfalls noch darzustellen sein wird, Elemente der Planung enthält, ja bei etwas groBzügiger Auslegung sogar mit der Planung gleichgesetzt werden kann. Ahnlicher Meinung ist auch Kosiol, der offensichtlich dem Planungselement in der Operations Research groBe Bedeutung beimiBt. Er geht von der Planungsforschung aus, stellt die Programm- und Verfahrensforschung zur Debatte, modifiziert den letzten Ausdruck zu Programm- und Verfahrensplanung, um sich schlielich unter dem Eindruck der immer wieder betonten Aufgabe der Operations Research, nämlich Unterlage für unternehmerische Entscheidungen zu sein, für den Begriff ,,Entscheidungsforschung" zu entschlieBen. In bewunderswerter Konsequenz ist die Operations Research für ihn methodisch gesehen ein Entscheidungskalkül. Mit der Einbeziehung der Elemente: Planung, Rechnung, Entscheidung hat Kosiol das Wesen der Operations Research wohl am treffendsten umschrieben.
Trotz allem ist der Ausdruck ,, Entscheidungsforschung" sprachlich gesehen nicht sehr glücklich gewählt; denn es erfolgt ja keine Analyse der Entscheidung, was doch der Begriff ,Entscheidungsforschung" besagt, sondern eine Analyse der vor der Entscheidung liegenden Gegebenheiten und Geschehen. Daher ist es dem Sachverhalt entsprechender, von der wissenschaftlichen Vorbereitung der Entscheidungen als von einer Entscheidungsforschung selbst zu sprechen.
